messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa glances from the spotless clerk’s desk back to Vell, then stills the urge to fidget with her prayer beads. Her voice is quiet but clear.

“He died three days ago, and the ledgers are still in his room. Did Jassan die of fever, Master Vell?” She watches his face without seeming to. “And who has been into that room since? Is there a key, or are we to ask the cooper to open a dead man’s door?”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell leans an elbow on the counter, easy, but his eyes go to the empty desk and stay there a beat before coming back to Vell.

"A few things, Master Vell, so we don't come back with the wrong box or no box at all."

He counts them off on his fingers, not hurrying:

"One. How did Jassan die? Fever, a fall, a knife? If it's the last, someone may have wanted the same box, and I'd like to know that before I walk up his stairs."

"Two. What does the box look like? Size, colour, and the seal. Whose mark, what wax? And who holds the key? You, or was it on him?"

"Three. Who else knows it's there? The cooper, the landlord, family, anyone he owed? Has anyone been in the room since he died?"

"Four. Does the landlord know we're coming? I'd rather knock with your name than climb in with mine."

He taps the counter once, mirroring Vell. "And if someone's already carried it off, do you still want it found, or is the job done?"

While Vell answers, Pell watches his face and hands more than his words, to see whether he stiffens at any question or glances at the desk.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I rest my shield against my leg, keeping a hand on its rim.

“A few practical things. How did Ferr die, and who holds the key to his room? We’ll want your written authority to collect the box.”

I meet Vell’s eyes. “And is anyone likely to dispute your claim to it? Seventy-five gold is generous for a short walk. I’d rather know what we’re being paid to face.”

scenes.narration:
Vell does not look at the desk. He keeps his eyes on whoever is speaking and waits until all three have finished before he answers. He takes the questions in the order he likes, not the order they were asked.

"His heart." He says it to Sefa first. "Not fever. Wenna Pike, the landlady, found him in the morning, in his chair. The Song of the Morning sent a priest to look at him. There was no mark on him. They buried him yesterday. I paid for it." He gives Pell a short glance. "No knife, Master Dunmore. If there had been one, the Fist would be in that room and you would not."

He spreads his fingers on the counter, as if measuring. "Oak, iron at the corners, about the length of my forearm. Two handles. It's heavy. One of you will want to carry it with both arms." He touches his waistcoat over the breastbone, where something small and hard sits under the cloth. "I have the key. Not him. Nobody opens it on the way, so nobody needs a key." Then he answers the seal question, a little faster than the others, the way a man says a thing he has already said to himself: "My seal is over the lock. Red-brown wax, a V in a ring. You will see it."

"Who else knows the box is there?" He thinks about it honestly. "Wenna Pike. She has the key to his room, so you ask her. The cooper downstairs, Tobin, perhaps. Jassan had no family here. His mother was a clerk in the Gate, and she has been dead for years." He pauses. Pell sees his thumb press flat against the wood, once. "Anyone he owed, I don't know. He didn't tell me his debts. If Wenna wants his rent, that is Jassan's debt. Not mine."

To Bram he gives the longest look. "Dispute it? The ledgers are mine. The box is mine." He breathes out through his nose. "There is a man on the Trade Way named Gerrit Thale. He lends money, as I do, and he would like very much to read my books. He has not been told about this box. That does not mean he hasn't heard. That is part of the seventy-five. The rest is haste, and keeping quiet. My clients' sums are my clients' business."

He has not answered the last question yet. When he does, he turns to Pell. "If someone has carried it off, find it. Same terms. Same nightfall."

He takes a sheet from under the counter, uncaps his own inkwell and writes four lines in a small, upright hand. He doesn't hesitate over any of the words. He folds the sheet twice, warms a stick of red-brown wax over the lamp and presses a ring from his left hand into it: a V inside a circle, neat and shallow. He slides the note to the middle of the counter, where any of them could take it. It says that the bearers act for Ostrin Vell and are to receive Jassan Ferr's strongbox.

"Show that to Wenna Pike. Follow the Coast Way past the third smithy; the cooper's yard has barrels stacked at the gate." He pulls the brass scales toward him and sets a weight in the pan, and he is already a moneylender at his morning work. Outside the shutters the hammers keep ringing. The light has moved a hand's width along the ledgers on the shelf. Beside him the clerk's stool stays pushed in under the empty desk.

 No roll was needed: these were questions put to Vell, and he answered them in the scene. He skipped two of them, so here are his answers:

"Who has been in the room since?" Vell sets the weight down. "Wenna. The priest who looked at him. The two men who carried him down to the temple. I have not been up there." He says the last part flatly. "Does she know you're coming? No. I sent no word. Show her the note."

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell picks up the note, checks the wax with a thumbnail without breaking it, and tucks it inside his jerkin. One more question on his way off the counter, casual, as if it only just occurred to him:

"When did you put your seal on that box, Master Vell? Before he took it home, or after?" He lets that sit a heartbeat. "Just so I know whether the wax we find should be fresh or three days old."

Whatever the answer, he nods, glances once more at the tidy desk, and taps the counter. "Before nightfall, then."

Outside, among the hammers, he falls in beside Sefa and Bram and speaks low as they walk toward the Coast Way:

"He answered the seal question before I'd finished asking it, and he's never set foot in that room. If someone's opened that box and resealed it, he'll say it was us. So nobody touches the box till all three of us have looked at the wax together. Agreed?"

As they go he keeps his eyes on the street, watching for anyone who lingers outside Vell's door or falls in behind them. If Thale has heard about the box, he may have a man watching the counting-house.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I take the letter and tuck it safely into my belt pouch.

“If the seal’s already broken when we find it, we’ll bring it as it stands. I won’t promise you someone else’s good behaviour.”

Outside, I wait for Sefa and Pell before setting off toward the cooper’s yard.

“I can carry the weight. That leaves my hands occupied, though—keep an eye on the street when we bring it back.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa takes the sealed note carefully by the edges, turns it once to be sure the wax is whole, and tucks it inside her sleeve. She meets Vell’s eye for a heartbeat.

“We’ll be back before evening. If someone has already opened it, you’ll know the instant we do.” A pause, not quite a smile. “We’ll keep your box whole, Master Vell; you keep your scales honest.”

She glances toward the tidy empty desk, then to Pell and Bram, and tilts her head toward the door.

“I want to see that room before half of Beregost hears three hired hands are asking after a dead man’s ledgers.”

Pell Dunmore: Pell picks up the note, checks the wax with a thumbnail without breaking it, and tucks it inside his jerkin. One more question on his way off the counter, casual, as if it only just occurred to him:

"When did you put your seal on that box, Master Vell? Before he took it home, or after?" He lets that sit a heartbeat. "Just so I know whether the wax we find should be fresh or three days old."

Whatever the answer, he nods, glances once more at the tidy desk, and taps the counter. "Before nightfall, then."

Outside, among the hammers, he falls in beside Sefa and Bram and speaks low as they walk toward the Coast Way:

"He answered the seal question before I'd finished asking it, and he's never set foot in that room. If someone's opened that box and resealed it, he'll say it was us. So nobody touches the box till all three of us have looked at the wax together. Agreed?"

As they go he keeps his eyes on the street, watching for anyone who lingers outside Vell's door or falls in behind them. If Thale has heard about the box, he may have a man watching the counting-house.

Bram Halloway: I take the letter and tuck it safely into my belt pouch.

“If the seal’s already broken when we find it, we’ll bring it as it stands. I won’t promise you someone else’s good behaviour.”

Outside, I wait for Sefa and Pell before setting off toward the cooper’s yard.

“I can carry the weight. That leaves my hands occupied, though—keep an eye on the street when we bring it back.”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa takes the sealed note carefully by the edges, turns it once to be sure the wax is whole, and tucks it inside her sleeve. She meets Vell’s eye for a heartbeat.

“We’ll be back before evening. If someone has already opened it, you’ll know the instant we do.” A pause, not quite a smile. “We’ll keep your box whole, Master Vell; you keep your scales honest.”

She glances toward the tidy empty desk, then to Pell and Bram, and tilts her head toward the door.

“I want to see that room before half of Beregost hears three hired hands are asking after a dead man’s ledgers.”

scenes.narration:
Pell is closest to the counter, and his hand gets to the note first. He runs a thumbnail along the edge of the wax without lifting it and slips the sheet inside his jerkin. Bram and Sefa reach for it a moment later and find bare wood.

Vell watches the note go and answers Pell's question in the same breath. "Before. Here, on this counter, the evening before he died. My ring, my wax. I locked it and he carried it home." His hand moves to his waistcoat, over the breastbone, then away. "I wanted it out of this house for a few days. That is my reason, and it stays mine. The wax will be four days old."

He turns to Bram. "As it stands, then. If it's broken, bring it broken. Then I'll know." To Sefa he gives a short, dry look, and the corner of his mouth doesn't move. "The town checks my scales every spring, Mistress Marrin. They have never been found light." He is already looking down at the weights when the door closes behind the three of them.

Outside, the Coast Way is full of noise and smoke. A cart of pig iron grinds past, and its driver shouts at a dog. Two apprentices carry a quench-tub between them with water slopping over the rim. A woman is beating a rug from an upstairs window. Pell looks down the street and back the way they came, at doorways, corners and the bench outside the chandler's. A carter is watering his mule. An old man sleeps against a wall in the sun. No one is waiting outside Vell's door, and no one starts walking when they do. Nothing in the street seems to care about three hirelings and a folded note.

They count the smithies. The third one is a farrier's, open to the street, where a horse stands with one hoof up and a boy holds its head. Past it the noise thins. The cooper's yard is where Vell said: a plank gate standing half open, with new barrels stacked three high on either side and the smell of shavings and wet oak coming out of it. Inside, someone is hammering hoops in a slow, steady rhythm. A wooden stair climbs the outside wall of the house to a door on the upper floor.

The left gatepost has been chalked low down, about knee height, where a passer-by's eye wouldn't go. It's a small circle with a short stroke through it and a dot above. Anyone who learned the marks on the roofs of the Wide would read it at once: *this house is being watched.* The chalk is fresh. Yesterday's rain hasn't touched it.

A woman's voice comes down the stair from the half-open door above, sharp, worn thin by repeating itself: "I've told you once already. Nothing leaves that room till I'm paid."

A man answers her, too low to make out.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I catch Pell’s eye and point briefly to the chalk mark, leaving it untouched.

Then I step through the gate toward the foot of the stairs, my sword sheathed.

“Mistress Pike? Bram Halloway. My companions and I have a letter from Ostrin Vell concerning his strongbox.”

I look up toward the doorway, trying to get a clear view of the man speaking with her. “Sounds as though we ought to talk before anything gets carried away.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa halts just short of the gate, drawing back a step into the shadow of the barrel stack. Her eyes go from the chalk mark to the half-open door above, then back.

“Pell,” she says very low, without turning her head. “Fresh chalk, knee-high on the post. Circle, a slash through it, a dot above. That isn’t the cooper’s mark.” She keeps her hands still at her sides, not near the dagger. “I don’t like walking into an argument on a dead man’s stair. If you can read it, say so now. Otherwise we do this polite and watch our hands.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops short of the gate as if to shake a stone from his boot, crouching, and takes a good look at the chalk without touching it. Then he straightens and speaks low to the other two, barely moving his lips:

"Chalk on the post. Thieves' mark, fresh today. 'This house is watched.' Somebody's working it." He tilts his head at the stair. "And somebody's up there now, wanting into that room before us."

He thinks for half a breath, then lays it out quickly:

"Bram, you go up the stair with the note, plain and loud, Vell's man come for Vell's box. Sefa with you; she's got the face for a landlady. I'll come up quiet behind you and hang back on the stair, out of sight. I want a look at our friend and a listen to what he says before he knows there's three of us."

He leaves the chalk as it is. Scrubbing it would only tell whoever made it that someone can read it. Before following, he lets his eyes go once around the yard and the street behind them. Who has a view of this gate and that stair? A window across the way, a loft door, someone idling where nobody idles? Then he slips in after the others and takes the stair close to the wall, where the treads creak least, stopping just below the landing where he can see through the half-open door without being seen.

He keeps his hand off his sword, but near it.

screens.Pell Dunmore:
Bram caught your eye and pointed briefly at the chalk mark, leaving it untouched. Then he went through the half-open gate with his sword sheathed and his shield on his arm. The yard smells of wet oak and shavings, and a brazier stands there for heating hoops. At the back a broad, bald man in a leather apron stands at a hooping block with a mallet raised. When he saw Bram, the mallet stayed up. At the foot of the outside stair Bram called up the wall, in a voice made for carrying down a line of wagons, to a Mistress Pike. He gave his name, said that he and his companions had a letter from Ostrin Vell about his strongbox, and added that they ought to talk before anything got carried away.

The argument upstairs stopped dead. The cooper brought his mallet down on the hoop once more, carefully, as if he had never paused.

Sefa stepped back into the narrow shade beside the barrel stack, her hands still at her sides and her eyes on the door above. She spoke to you very low. She had noticed the fresh chalk on the post, knee-high, a circle with a slash through it and a dot above, and she said it wasn't the cooper's mark. She was uneasy about walking into a quarrel on the stair of a dead man's house. If you could read the mark, you should say so now. Otherwise they would do this politely and watch their hands.

You crouched by the post as if you had a stone in your boot, read the chalk without having to think, and told them in a few low words what it meant and what you wanted done. Then you straightened and looked the street over once. The house opposite has its shutters closed. A stable loft door two buildings down is bolted from outside. Three children are chasing a hoop down the middle of the road, and a woman is shouting at them about the carts. Nobody is idling, nobody leans in a doorway, and no window stands open with no one in it. Whoever chalked that post isn't watching from the street.

You slip through the gate behind Bram and take the stair on the wall side, where the treads are nailed tightest. Every eye above is turned toward the man in mail at the bottom.

scenes.input:
(Round 3 — one paragraph per character in this scene. Close this scene on the world as it stands: no question, offer, demand or wait put to one character, and no out-of-game note — the table asks every player what they do next.)

Bram Halloway: I catch Pell’s eye and point briefly to the chalk mark, leaving it untouched.

Then I step through the gate toward the foot of the stairs, my sword sheathed.

“Mistress Pike? Bram Halloway. My companions and I have a letter from Ostrin Vell concerning his strongbox.”

I look up toward the doorway, trying to get a clear view of the man speaking with her. “Sounds as though we ought to talk before anything gets carried away.”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa halts just short of the gate, drawing back a step into the shadow of the barrel stack. Her eyes go from the chalk mark to the half-open door above, then back.

“Pell,” she says very low, without turning her head. “Fresh chalk, knee-high on the post. Circle, a slash through it, a dot above. That isn’t the cooper’s mark.” She keeps her hands still at her sides, not near the dagger. “I don’t like walking into an argument on a dead man’s stair. If you can read it, say so now. Otherwise we do this polite and watch our hands.”

Pell Dunmore: Pell stops short of the gate as if to shake a stone from his boot, crouching, and takes a good look at the chalk without touching it. Then he straightens and speaks low to the other two, barely moving his lips:

"Chalk on the post. Thieves' mark, fresh today. 'This house is watched.' Somebody's working it." He tilts his head at the stair. "And somebody's up there now, wanting into that room before us."

He thinks for half a breath, then lays it out quickly:

"Bram, you go up the stair with the note, plain and loud, Vell's man come for Vell's box. Sefa with you; she's got the face for a landlady. I'll come up quiet behind you and hang back on the stair, out of sight. I want a look at our friend and a listen to what he says before he knows there's three of us."

He leaves the chalk as it is. Scrubbing it would only tell whoever made it that someone can read it. Before following, he lets his eyes go once around the yard and the street behind them. Who has a view of this gate and that stair? A window across the way, a loft door, someone idling where nobody idles? Then he slips in after the others and takes the stair close to the wall, where the treads creak least, stopping just below the landing where he can see through the half-open door without being seen.

He keeps his hand off his sword, but near it.

"Pell," she says, hardly louder than the hammering. "Fresh chalk, knee-high on the post. Circle, a slash through it, a dot above. That isn't the cooper's mark. I don't like walking into an argument on a dead man's stair. If you can read it, say so now. Otherwise we do this polite and watch our hands."

Pell has crouched by the post as if he had a stone in his boot. He reads the chalk the way he read such marks at twelve, without having to think. He tells the two of them what it says in a few low words and lays out his plan. Then he straightens up and looks the street over once. The house opposite has its shutters closed. A stable loft door two buildings down is bolted from outside. Three children are chasing a hoop down the middle of the road, and a woman is shouting at them about the carts. Nobody is idling, nobody is leaning in a doorway, and no window is open with no one in it. Whoever chalked that post isn't watching from the street. Pell slips through the gate behind Bram and takes the stair on the wall side, where the treads are nailed tightest, while every eye above is turned toward the man in mail at the bottom.

Near the top, a third of the way up from the landing, one tread is new pale pine, nailed over the stump of an old one. It sits a finger higher than the rest. Pell's heel catches its edge and the plank gives a dry crack under him. In the noise of the yard it's a small sound, but nobody up there is talking.

A woman steps out onto the landing first: thin, about fifty, sleeves pushed to the elbow, a ring of keys hanging from her belt on a leather thong. She looks down over the rail at Bram. A man moves into the half-open doorway behind her, unhurried, and his eyes go straight down the stair to Pell, three treads below his boots.

He is past forty, lean, with grey hair cropped close and a nose that was broken once and set a little crooked. He wears a good plain coat and has a short cudgel hooked in his belt. He holds a small purse in his left hand, half open, the way a man holds something he has been showing. He looks at Pell a breath longer than he needs to, the way you look at a face you think you ought to know. Then he smiles.

"Mind that one, friend. It's new." His voice is soft and pleasant, and the vowels come straight off the Lower City docks of the Gate. "The old one went through under the men carrying him down." He looks down at Bram, then past him to the barrel stack where Sefa stands in the shade, and he counts the three of them without hiding that he's counting. He speaks to the landlady without raising his voice. "Three of them now, mistress. My offer hasn't changed, and it's in my hand. Theirs is a letter."

Wenna Pike doesn't look round at him. She grips the rail and speaks down to Bram in the same thin, worn voice. "Halloway. I don't know you. I know Jassan Ferr owed me three gold and four silver. I know his master paid the temple to bury him and never sent me a copper for the room he died in. I've sold the man's good coat to cover part of it, and I'm not ashamed of that." Her other hand closes over the keys at her belt. "Nothing leaves that room till I'm paid. I said it to him and I'll say it to you, Vell's letter or no."

Behind her, through the gap at the hinge side of the door, Pell can see a slice of the room. There's the corner of a narrow bed and a cold grate with ash in it. On the floor beside a chair is something squared and dark, with iron at its corners. Below, the cooper's mallet strikes the hoop, and strikes it again.

He looks down at Bram, then past him to the barrel stack where Sefa stands in the shade, and he counts the three of them without hiding that he's counting. He speaks to the landlady without raising his voice. "Three of them now, mistress. My offer hasn't changed, and it's in my hand. Theirs is a letter."

Wenna Pike doesn't look round at him. She grips the rail and speaks down to Bram in the same thin, worn voice. "Halloway. I don't know you. I know Jassan Ferr owed me three gold and four silver. Bram caught your eye and pointed briefly at the chalk mark, leaving it untouched. Then he went through the half-open gate with his sword sheathed and his shield on his arm. The yard smells of wet oak and shavings, and a brazier stands there for heating hoops. At the back a broad, bald man in a leather apron stands at a hooping block with a mallet raised. When he saw Bram, the mallet stayed up. At the foot of the outside stair Bram called up the wall, in a voice made for carrying down a line of wagons, to a Mistress Pike. He gave his name, said that he and his companions had a letter from Ostrin Vell about his strongbox, and added that they ought to talk before anything got carried away.

The argument upstairs stopped dead. The cooper brought his mallet down on the hoop once more, carefully, as if he had never paused.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps out from the shadow of the barrel stack and crosses to the foot of the stair, her hands open and away from her blade. She looks from Pike to the grey-haired man, then back to the landlady.

“Then let’s settle the honest claim before anyone carries anything.” She works three gold and four silver from her purse and holds them up in the morning light. “Jassan’s arrears, Mistress Pike — counted into your hand before we set foot on your stair. That makes the room yours to open for us and Master Vell’s property his to reclaim. If there’s more of Jassan’s about, you keep it against the rest.”

She doesn’t raise her voice. But when she meets the stranger’s eyes, her tone thins a little. “I don’t know your name, and you don’t have to give it. But if that purse was bid on a red-brown seal, you’re late. The box in that room was never Jassan’s to sell.” Her eyes drop pointedly to his hands, then back to his face. “It goes back whole, or not at all.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes the last three treads without hurrying, stepping over the new pine one with exaggerated care, and gives the grey-haired man a small nod as if thanking him for the warning.

"Kind of you." He holds the man's eyes a moment, friendly, then lets a phrase fall in passing, light as weather talk but in the cadence of the roofs: *"Chalk's still wet at the gate."* In cant it means *I've seen your mark, and I know whose house this is.* He watches how the man takes it: a flicker, a glance at the post, nothing at all.

Then he turns his shoulder to him and speaks to the landlady, quiet and plain.

"Mistress Pike. Three gold and four silver, you said." He's already untying his purse. He counts it out onto the rail in front of her, coin by coin where she can see each one: three gold, four silver. "There. Jassan's rent, paid. Not Vell's money. Mine. I'll take it out of his hide later, that's my lookout." A short, crooked smile. "You've been owed long enough, and you shouldn't have to auction a dead man's room on your own stair."

He leaves his hand flat beside the coins without pushing them at her.

"All I ask is a word that the debt's settled, so nobody comes back saying otherwise. And tell me true: since they carried him down, has anyone been inside that room besides you? Has anyone touched the box or moved it from where it sits?"

He keeps the grey-haired man at the edge of his sight the whole time, watching the hand with the purse and the hand near the cudgel, and stays a step to the side so the man isn't between him and the stair.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I fold Odda’s letter and put it away. For a moment I keep my hand over the pouch, then turn my attention back to the landing.

“Three gold and four silver. I’ll pay it, Mistress Pike, if that settles the room debt in full. You’ll give me a receipt, and let the three of us inspect the box before it’s moved.”

I leave my purse at my belt for now and look at the man with the cudgel.

“You’ve heard my name. What’s yours, and whose business brings you to Ferr’s room?”

scenes.narration:
Pell gets there first. Sefa is still at the foot of the stair with three gold and four silver held up in the light, and Bram has only started to speak, when Pell steps over the new pine tread with exaggerated care and comes up level with the landing. As he passes the grey-haired man he nods to him, friendly.

"Kind of you." He holds the man's eyes a moment and lets a phrase drop as lightly as talk about the weather, in the up-and-down rhythm of the Wide's roofs. "Chalk's still wet at the gate."

The man's face barely moves. His eyes go once to Pell's face, slower this time, the way you look again at a coin you think you've seen before. Then the corner of his mouth lifts and he answers in the same rhythm, so softly that only Pell catches the cant under it. "Mind your feet on it, then." On the roofs that means *it's mine, and I saw you first.* He doesn't glance at the gatepost. He doesn't need to.

Pell turns his shoulder to him and lays the coins on the rail in front of Wenna Pike one at a time, three gold and four silver, where she can watch each one land. He tells her whose money it is and asks for a word that the debt is settled. Then he leaves his hand flat beside the coins.

Wenna looks at them for a long moment. She doesn't count them twice. She sweeps them into her palm, closes her fist and pushes it into her apron pocket. For the first time that morning her shoulders come down.

"I know three gold and four silver when I see it," she says. She leans over the rail and her thin voice cuts across the yard. "Tobin! You heard. Jassan Ferr's room is paid up."

The mallet stops at the back of the yard. "Heard," the cooper calls, and starts again.

"There's your word, and a witness to it. I can write my name, Halloway, if you want it on paper as well." She gives Bram that much, then looks down at Sefa and at the coins still in her raised hand. "Keep yours. I'm paid, and I won't take it twice." She looks at Bram's purse, still at his belt. "Same for you."

She answers Pell's question without being asked a second time. "Since they carried him down? Me. The priest, Brother Aldane from the Song, who looked him over. The two that carried him. Nobody's moved that box. I dusted round it and left it where he left it, beside his chair." She tilts her head at the man in the doorway without looking at him. "This one's been up twice with his purse. He's stood in that doorway. He hasn't been past it. Not while I'm on this stair."

Sefa's words to the stranger have stayed with him, and he answers her first, over the rail and down the stair, as easily as if she'd asked the time. "Red-brown, is it." He seems to taste the words. His eyes slide back through the gap at the hinge side of the door, toward the floor by the chair, and when they come back the small smile is still there. He doesn't say anything else about the seal.

Then he looks at Bram. "Coll. Brannock, if you want all of it." He closes the purse and hooks it on his belt next to the cudgel. "Whose business? A man who reads a ledger better than he reads a letter, friend, and who pays better than either. My offer to the mistress is done with, since you've paid her." He starts down the stair, unhurried. At the pine tread he steps wide, the way he told Pell to, and he moves to the wall side to get past Bram and Sefa. "Have your look at the wax. All three of you, the way careful people do. When you've had it, you'll want to hear what my man pays for a box carried by Vell's own hands. I won't be far." He reaches the gate, stops beside the chalked post and looks back up at the landing. "It's a long way down the Coast Way with both arms full."

He goes out into the street, and the noise of the smithies takes him.

Wenna pulls the leather thong off her belt, picks out a dark iron key from the ring and turns it in Jassan Ferr's lock. The door swings fully open on a room that smells of cold ash and old paper. There's a narrow bed, made tight. On the nightstand beside it stands a small dark vial, and a stain has dried on the floorboards just below it. The grate is cold, and the ash in it is grey, with a curl of something blacker in it that kept its shape when it burned. A single chair faces the window. Beside it on the floor sits the oak strongbox with iron at its corners, a blob of wax over its lock, exactly where a man would set it down so that it was the last thing his hand found before he slept.

"Look all you like," Wenna says, and steps back against the rail to let them pass.

 (Out of game) Paying Wenna's rent was a plain handover of coin with nothing uncertain about it, so it needed no roll; she took the money, as the scene showed.

(Out of game) Thieves' Cant is on Pell's sheet, and there was nothing uncertain about saying a cant line or seeing how Coll took it: he answered openly in cant, so that needed no roll either.

Sefa is still at the foot of the stair with three gold and four silver held up in the light, and Bram has only started to speak, when Pell steps over the new pine tread with exaggerated care and comes up level with the landing. As he passes the grey-haired man he nods to him, friendly.

"Kind of you." He holds the man's eyes a moment and lets a phrase drop as lightly as talk about the weather, in the up-and-down rhythm of the Wide's roofs. "Chalk's still wet at the gate."

The man's face barely moves. His eyes go once to Pell's face, slower this time, the way you look again at a coin you think you've seen before. Then the corner of his mouth lifts and he answers in the same rhythm, so softly that only Pell catches the cant under it. "Mind your feet on it, then." On the roofs that means *it's mine, and I saw you first.* He doesn't glance at the gatepost. He doesn't need to.

Pell turns his shoulder to him and lays the coins on the rail in front of Wenna Pike one at a time, three gold and four silver, where she can watch each one land. He tells her whose money it is and asks for a word that the debt is settled. Then he leaves his hand flat beside the coins.

Wenna looks at them for a long moment. She doesn't count them twice. She sweeps them into her palm, closes her fist and pushes it into her apron pocket. For the first time that morning her shoulders come down.

"I know three gold and four silver when I see it," she says. She leans over the rail and her thin voice cuts across the yard. "Tobin! You heard. Jassan Ferr's room is paid up."

The mallet stops at the back of the yard. "Heard," the cooper calls, and starts again.

"There's your word, and a witness to it. I can write my name, Halloway, if you want it on paper as well." She gives Bram that much, then looks down at Sefa and at the coins still in her raised hand. "Keep yours. I'm paid, and I won't take it twice." She looks at Bram's purse, still at his belt. "Same for you."

She answers Pell's question without being asked a second time. "Since they carried him down? Me. The priest, Brother Aldane from the Song, who looked him over. The two that carried him. Nobody's moved that box. I dusted round it and left it where he left it, beside his chair." She tilts her head at the man in the doorway without looking at him. "This one's been up twice with his purse. He's stood in that doorway. He hasn't been past it. Not while I'm on this stair."

Sefa's words to the stranger have stayed with him, and he answers her first, over the rail and down the stair, as easily as if she'd asked the time. "Red-brown, is it." He seems to taste the words. His eyes slide back through the gap at the hinge side of the door, toward the floor by the chair, and when they come back the small smile is still there. He doesn't say anything else about the seal.

Then he looks at Bram. "Coll. Brannock, if you want all of it." He closes the purse and hooks it on his belt next to the cudgel. "Whose business? A man who reads a ledger better than he reads a letter, friend, and who pays better than either. My offer to the mistress is done with, since you've paid her." He starts down the stair, unhurried. At the pine tread he steps wide, the way he told Pell to, and he moves to the wall side to get past Bram and Sefa. "Have your look at the wax. All three of you, the way careful people do. When you've had it, you'll want to hear what my man pays for a box carried by Vell's own hands. I won't be far." He reaches the gate, stops beside the chalked post and looks back up at the landing. "It's a long way down the Coast Way with both arms full."

He goes out into the street, and the noise of the smithies takes him.

Wenna pulls the leather thong off her belt, picks out a dark iron key from the ring and turns it in Jassan Ferr's lock. The door swings fully open on a room that smells of cold ash and old paper. There's a narrow bed, made tight. On the nightstand beside it stands a small dark vial, and a stain has dried on the floorboards just below it. The grate is cold, and the ash in it is grey, with a curl of something blacker in it that kept its shape when it burned. A single chair faces the window. Beside it on the floor sits the oak strongbox with iron at its corners, a blob of wax over its lock, exactly where a man would set it down so that it was the last thing his hand found before he slept.

"Look all you like," Wenna says, and steps back against the rail to let them pass.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops in the doorway and doesn't go in yet. He looks back down the stair and lifts two fingers to Bram and Sefa: *up, both of you.* He waits until they're on the landing, so the three of them enter together, as agreed.

"Nobody touches the box," he says quietly. "Look first."

He crouches by the strongbox without laying a hand on it and studies the wax from a hand's breadth away, letting the window light slant across it. Is the V in the ring crisp or smeared? Are the edges cracked or lifted, is there a second layer, a seam, a softer colour where it was warmed again? Are the lock and the iron corners scratched, the hinges or the wood around the hasp marked, the dust on the floor disturbed?

"Sefa, Bram. Your eyes on this too, before anyone carries it."

Then he turns to the rest of the room, slow and methodical:

- **The vial.** He looks first without lifting it. Is there a label, a stopper, anything left inside? Then he picks it up by the neck with a cloth from his sleeve, holds it to the light, and waves a breath of air from it toward his nose. He doesn't put his face to it.
- **The stain** below it. Spilled, or dropped? Which way did it run?
- **The grate.** He crouches and teases the black curl out with the tip of a dagger, gently, so it doesn't crumble. Paper, parchment, a letter? Is any writing or a seal mark still showing? He looks through the ash for anything else that didn't burn.
- **The chair facing the window.** What's in reach of it? What would a man see sitting there? Anything tucked in the cushion or under it?

Over his shoulder, to Wenna, still mild: "Mistress, was that vial his? Medicine, something from the temple? And the grate: was it lit the night he died, or did someone burn something in it after?"

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Thank you, Mistress Pike. Your word and Tobin’s witness will do.”

I climb the stairs, minding the raised tread, and stop inside the room without touching anything.

“Pell, I’ll owe you my share of the rent. And Coll’s warning means we shouldn’t leave here with our hands full and no plan.”

I crouch beside the box to examine the wax with the others: the impression, its edges, and any cracks or signs it has been lifted or warmed. I leave the handles alone.

Then I glance toward the vial and the stain. “Mistress Pike, do you know what Ferr was taking? Was that bottle here when you found him?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa crosses the threshold after Wenna steps back, but stops just inside the door with her hands folded at her waist, plainly not touching anything. Her eyes move slowly over the made bed, the cold grate, the dark vial and the stain beneath it, then settle on the strongbox by the chair.

“No one puts a hand on that until all three of us have looked at the wax, from both sides,” she says quietly, for Pell and Bram as much as herself. Then she points with two fingers, not quite at the things, at the tale of the room. “But the seal isn’t the only thing in here that tells a story. A heart can stop in a bottle, and someone burned something in that grate they didn’t want to burn.”

She turns her head toward the landing, an edge of the old hospice in her voice. “Mistress Pike — did Jassan take physick for his heart? And did you find the room just as you left it, or had you tided before Brother Aldane saw him?”

screens.Pell Dunmore:
Bram comes up the stair after your signal, stepping wide over the raised pine tread, and Sefa follows close behind him. On the landing Bram thanks Mistress Pike, saying her word and Tobin's witness will do. He tells you quietly that he'll owe you his share of the rent, and that after Coll's warning the three of you shouldn't leave with full hands and no plan.

You go in together. Sefa stops a pace past the threshold, hands clasped in front of her. Her eyes travel over the bed, the cold grate, the vial and the stain, and settle on the box. She says quietly that no one lays a hand on it until all three have looked at the wax. She points two fingers toward the nightstand and the grate, and says the seal is not the only thing in the room with a tale to tell: a heart can fail inside a bottle, and someone put to the fire in that grate something they did not want to survive.

You crouch a hand's breadth from the box. Bram kneels across from you, his shield set against the bedframe, and Sefa bends over the two of you. The window light comes in low across the floorboards and the lock.

None of you needs long to see it.

The wax isn't red-brown. It's dark green, the colour of old bottle glass, poured over a flat disc of lead pressed into the keyhole plate. There's no V in it and no ring. The stamp shows a pair of balance scales, and under the beam where the pans hang is a single shut eye, its lid drawn in one fine curved line. The impression is crisp. The edges are whole, with no cracks, no lifted rim, no second layer and no soft patch where the wax was warmed again. Whoever sealed this did it once and did it well. The iron corners have only old knocks, nothing bright or fresh. The hasp and the wood round the lock are unmarked. Wenna's dusting has left a clean square of floor around the box, so nobody can say whose feet stood there before her.

With your face low to it, you see something more in the slanting light. Inside the green, under the surface, there's a faint grain of whorls, like a thumb pad pressed against glass. Nobody pressed a thumb into this wax. The lines run inside it, too even to be dust and too fine for a tool, and when you tilt your head the grain shifts with the light.

You leave the box where it is and start on the room. You pick the vial up by its neck through a cloth from your sleeve. It's dark brown glass with the cork pushed in and no label, and a finger's depth of liquid moves at the bottom. You ease the cork out and waft the air toward your nose. It's bitter and green, like crushed leaves steeped in spirit, and it catches at the back of your throat. You put the cork back. The stain below the nightstand is a splash, not a pool, thrown outward in a fan with a few dark drops toward the chair, the shape something makes when it's knocked off an edge and hits the boards.

Then you go to the grate and work the tip of your dagger under the black curl, slowly, to lift it out of the ash without crushing it.

The stamp shows a pair of balance scales, and under the beam where the pans hang is a single eye, shut, its lid drawn in one fine curved line. The impression is crisp. The edges are whole, with no cracks, no lifted rim, no second layer and no soft patch where the wax was warmed again. Whoever sealed this did it once and did it well. The iron corners have the usual old knocks and nothing bright or fresh. The hasp and the wood round the lock are unmarked. Wenna's dusting has left a clean square of floor around the box, so nobody can say whose feet stood there before her.

Pell has his face low to it, and he sees something else in the slanting light. Inside the green, under the surface, there's a faint grain like whorls, the way the pad of a thumb looks pressed against glass. But nobody pressed a thumb into this wax. The lines run *inside* it, too even to be dust and too fine for a tool. When he tilts his head the grain shifts a little with the light.

Pell leaves the box where it is and starts on the room. He picks the vial up by its neck through a cloth from his sleeve. It's dark brown glass with the cork pushed in and no label, and a finger's depth of liquid moves at the bottom. He eases the cork out and wafts the air toward his nose. It's bitter and green, like crushed leaves steeped in spirit, and it catches at the back of his throat. He puts the cork back. The stain below the nightstand is a splash, not a pool. It's thrown outward in a fan, with a few dark drops toward the chair, the shape something makes when it's knocked off an edge and hits the boards.

Then he goes to the grate and works the tip of a dagger under the black curl, slowly, to lift it out of the ash without crushing it.

Pell stops on the threshold. Before he goes in he looks back down the stair and lifts two fingers to the others: *up, both of you.*

Bram comes up first. "Thank you, Mistress Pike. Your word and Tobin's witness will do." He steps wide over the pine tread the way Coll did, and the stair groans under his mail. Sefa follows close behind. On the landing Bram stops beside Pell and keeps his voice down. "Pell, I'll owe you my share of the rent. And after Coll's warning, we shouldn't leave here with our hands full and no plan."

They go in together. Sefa stops a pace inside the door with her hands folded at her waist. Her eyes move over the tight bed, the cold grate, the vial and the stain, and come to rest on the box. "No one puts a hand on that until all three of us have looked at the wax, from both sides," she says quietly. She points two fingers toward the nightstand and then the grate without quite pointing at either. "But the seal isn't the only thing in here with a story to tell. A heart can stop in a bottle. And somebody burned something in that grate they didn't want burned."

"Nobody touches the box," Pell says. "Look first."

He crouches a hand's breadth from it, with Bram down on one knee across from him, his shield set against the bedframe. Sefa bends over the two of them. The window light comes in low across the floorboards and over the lock.

None of the three needs long to see it.

The wax isn't red-brown. It's dark green, the colour of old bottle glass, and it's poured over a flat disc of lead pressed into the keyhole plate. There's no V in it and no ring. The stamp shows a pair of balance scales, and under the beam where the pans hang is a single eye, shut, its lid drawn in one fine curved line. The impression is crisp. The edges are whole, with no cracks, no lifted rim, no second layer and no soft patch where the wax was warmed again. Whoever sealed this did it once and did it well. The iron corners have the usual old knocks and nothing bright or fresh. The hasp and the wood round the lock are unmarked. Wenna's dusting has left a clean square of floor around the box, so nobody can say whose feet stood there before her.

It's dark brown glass with the cork pushed in and no label, and a finger's depth of liquid moves at the bottom. He eases the cork out and wafts the air toward his nose. It's bitter and green, like crushed leaves steeped in spirit, and it catches at the back of his throat. He puts the cork back. The stain below the nightstand is a splash, not a pool. It's thrown outward in a fan, with a few dark drops toward the chair, the shape something makes when it's knocked off an edge and hits the boards.

Then he goes to the grate and works the tip of a dagger under the black curl, slowly, to lift it out of the ash without crushing it.

Pell turns to the chair. It's a plain ladder-back with a flat, sat-down cushion. He lifts the cushion, runs his fingers along the seams and finds nothing, and puts it back the way it lay. Sitting there, a man would have the window straight in front of him, and through it the yard gate, the barrel stacks and a stretch of the Coast Way. The nightstand would be at his right hand and the box at his right foot. Pell keeps searching. He goes down on his belly beside the chair and looks along the boards under it at floor level, where the light runs flat.

One board under the chair's back legs isn't like the others. Its four nail heads are bright, scraped round the rims the way they look when a knife blade has levered them up and they've been tapped back down by hand. The dust in the cracks along both its edges is gone, as if it had been wiped, while the cracks of the boards on either side are packed grey. He presses one end with two fingers and the far end lifts a thumb's width. Through the gap, in the dark underneath, he sees the dull shine of oilcloth wrapped round something small and squared off, tucked between the joists. He lets the board settle back. The chair's legs stand on it, and a man sitting in that chair every night would have had it under his heels.

The grate goes worse. The black curl comes up on the dagger tip, holds for a breath, and then the heat-brittle sheet splits along its folds and falls into flakes. Most of it is ash before it reaches the hearthstone. One flake the size of a thumbnail lands face up. Pell can make out three letters in a careful, upright clerk's hand, *Serg*, with the rest of the word burned away. Then the draught from the door stirs the ash and the flake curls into it. Nothing else in the grate held its shape. It's grey wood ash, and paper ash on top of it.

From the doorway Wenna has heard all three of them asking, and she answers them together, counting it off.

"He took drops. Bitter muck, three in a cup of water before bed. He said it was for his chest. I'd hear him cough at the taste through the floor. Where he got it I never asked." She looks at the nightstand. "That bottle was on the boards by his foot when I came in, on its side with the cork half out. I pushed the cork in and stood it up after they took him. Before that I touched nothing but him. I closed his eyes. I know what I touched and what I didn't." Her hand goes to the keys at her belt and stays there. "The grate wasn't lit. It's been too warm for a fire all week. That last evening he came down with a taper for a light off Tobin's brazier, and after that I smelled paper burning up here, not wood. Nobody's burned anything since. I've been on that stair every day."

Below, Tobin's mallet keeps its slow beat on the hoop. In the window the Coast Way goes about its morning: a cart, a dog, the smoke from the smithies drifting low. On the floor the green seal holds the light with its closed eye, and under the chair the loose board sits flat again over the oilcloth.

 A word on the grate, to put it in order: Pell actually had two tries at it. On the first, the dagger tip slides under the curl at the wrong angle and catches a fold. A strip as wide as a finger breaks off the edge and goes to powder on the hearthstone before he can steady the blade. He breathes out, sets the dagger flat and tries again, slower, from the side where the sheet looks whole. The second try is the one that lifts it clear for a breath before it splits along its folds. His hands did everything right, but the paper had burned too far to hold, and of the whole sheet only that one thumbnail flake with *Serg* on it came out readable.

journal: Debt: Bram's share of Jassan's rent

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Before anyone lifts the box, I draw out Odda’s letter.

“There’s something you both need to see.” I keep my voice low and hold it for Sefa and Pell to read. “A boy slipped me this in the yard. Odda Brand says Vell will take her house over a debt her husband left. She wants a page removed.”

I look between them. “I’m not breaking the seal behind your backs. Nor do I much fancy delivering the means to put her out without finding out whether it’s true. Once we’ve checked this wax, we need to talk.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays just inside the door, her back to the jamb so she isn’t crowding the room. She doesn’t move toward the box yet; her eyes go from the seal to the window, then settle again on the dead man’s chair.

“Pell.” Her voice is low, almost at prayer-pitch. “You’ve the best eye for wax and locks. I’ll hold the light and the quiet while you look at it from both sides — the join, the edges, the keyhole. Bram, stand so the landing isn’t behind his back.”

She reaches out, not touching what she shouldn’t, and lets two fingers rest lightly on Pell’s sleeve. “The Lantern guide your hands,” she says, and a brief warmth passes from her fingers into his, the sort that settles in the hands and steadies them. It fades at once.

Then she shifts her attention to the room’s smaller story, moving one slow half-step at a time toward the nightstand without reaching for anything. She lowers her breathing.

“Mistress Pike,” she asks gently, “when you found him, was that window shut or open? And this vial — had you seen it before?” She nods toward the black curl in the cold ash. “Or did that burn sometime after they carried him down?”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell sits back on his heels and keeps his voice down, pitched for the two beside him and not the doorway.

"Three things. That's not Vell's seal. Green, scales, a shut eye, no V, and it's never been touched since it was poured. So either Vell lied to us about what's on his own box, or that's not the box he sealed." He nods at the wax. "And there's something living in it. Those lines move with the light. Sefa, does that look like magic to you? Can you tell what kind without touching it?"

scenes.narration:
Bram holds the letter low between his body and the window, so the doorway can't see the page. Odda Brand's handwriting is careful and a little cramped, like someone who doesn't write often and didn't want to waste the paper. Sefa and Pell read it over his arm:

*Bram — Harl died owing Ostrin Vell forty gold, and Vell's note for it is in his dead clerk's strongbox — the one Vell has hired you to bring him. Jassan wrote to me before he died: once the box is back, Vell calls the note and takes the house. If that one page were gone before Vell opened the box, there would be nothing to call. Please. I have no one else to ask. — Odda Brand*

Bram keeps his voice down. He tells them where it came from and what he won't do behind their backs. Out on the landing Wenna Pike has her elbows on the rail and her eyes on the yard. Under the noise of Tobin's mallet she doesn't hear a word.

Sefa stays with her back to the doorjamb. She rests two fingers on Pell's sleeve and says the words quietly. Warmth passes into his hands and stays there, steady and faint, the way a cup stays warm after the tea is drunk. Then she moves half a step at a time toward the nightstand and puts her questions to the landing.

Wenna turns round. "The window was shut. He kept it latched. Said the smoke off the smithies got into his papers. I opened it after they took him, to let the room air, and I shut it again." She looks at the vial. "That's stood on that nightstand since the thaw. He bought it in town somewhere, and I never asked where. The grate's the way he left it."

Pell tells the other two what he's found, the wax, the drops and the board, in three low points. He wraps the vial in his cloth and puts it in the healer's satchel, away from the red flasks. Wenna watches it go and doesn't object. Then Pell asks her in, and she comes to stand at the foot of the bed with her arms folded, where she can see his hands.

He lifts the chair aside and sets it down without a sound. Then he goes over the board slowly, the way he'd go over a sill on a second floor: the nail heads, the holes they came out of, the gap at the end, the crack along each side. There's no thread or pin, and no wire pulled tight across the dark underneath. Whoever lifted this board meant to hide something, not to trap anyone. Pell works the dagger point under the loose end. The nails come up the way they went in, already loosened, and the board lifts in his hand.

On the joist beside the bundle lie a few crumbs of dark green wax, small and dry, as if they had fallen off something set down there in a hurry.

The bundle comes out easily. It's about the size of a child's fist and far heavier than that, the dead weight of lead. Through the oilcloth Pell can feel the shape: one end flat and round, the width of a large coin, a short thick neck, and a knob at the other end to grip. It's tied twice round with waxed thread and finished in a small, tight knot, the kind clerks use on document bundles. There's no seal on it and nothing written on the cloth. He sets it on the floorboards in the window light, still wrapped. The warmth Sefa gave his hands fades while he works, and he never needed it.

Wenna looks at the hole in her floor and then at the bundle. "Twelve years I've let this room." Her mouth goes thin. "Whatever that is, it was his. It isn't mine. I'm paid, and I want no part of a dead man's hiding places."

She goes back to the doorway and stands in it. In the yard below the mallet goes on striking. On the floor the green seal on the box catches the light, and beside it lies the wrapped weight of lead, with an empty gap in the boards where it used to be.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn’t answer Pell at once. She crosses to the strongbox, going down on one knee beside it with her hands folded, studying the green wax from less than a hand’s width away. Her lips move once, silently — not a prayer, the habit of reading a wound before touching it.

“The lines shift like ink running under glass, not like light,” she says at last, half to herself. “If it’s magic, it’s a maker’s mark, not a snare — but I wouldn’t warm it with a thumb.” She leans back a little, careful not to breathe on the seal. “Scales and a shut eye: the old dockside mark for a blind bargain, a debt weighed in the dark. Vell didn’t pour this. It was stamped here, I think, and in a hurry.” Her eyes move to the few crumbs of green wax beside the hole in the floor. “The same stuff by the joist.”

She gets to her feet, and her voice picks up its old hospice calm, the one she kept when a bedside went quiet. “Open the bundle here. If it’s lead, it’s hiding something from scrying — a key, a paper, a name. If it’s trapped, better a spirit hand finds the needle than yours.” Her eyes go to Pell. “I can lift it with a mage hand, turn the tied side toward the light and keep my fingers out of the dark. You watch the knot and the board. If it’s clean, you open it. If it isn’t, we set it down, close the boards, and carry better questions to Vell.”

She levels two fingers toward the wrapped bundle and speaks a word that is more breath than voice. A pale, spectral hand gathers in the air above it, thin as morning incense-smoke, and waits.

Then, for Wenna’s benefit as much as theirs, she adds quietly: “You said the room smelled of old paper. It smells of old secrets to me.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell weighs the bundle in his palm through the oilcloth a moment, then sets it down and speaks low to the other two.

"I'd bet my share that's a seal. Flat round face, neck, a knob to grip. Lead, so it's cheap and it's private. And green wax crumbs on the joist beside it." He nods at the box. "Jassan sealed that himself, his own mark, then hid the stamp under his own feet. Vell's wax was gone before we ever got here."

He works the clerk's knot loose with his fingertips, slowly, so it can be tied again the same way, and folds back the oilcloth without lifting what's inside. He looks at the face of it in the window light. Is it the scales and the shut eye? Is it cut backward, as a stamp should be? He sets it beside the box, near the green wax but not touching it, so all three can compare. He doesn't press it to anything.

"Sefa, the lines in that wax, the ones that move. Is that magic? A ward, a mark that tells someone if it's broken? I'd like to know what we're carrying before we carry it."

Then, quieter still, to Bram, about the letter:

"Your widow's page. Think on this before you decide anything. Jassan wrote to her, Jassan broke Vell's seal and put his own on, and Jassan burned something in that grate the night he died. We don't know the note's even still in there." A glance at the box. "And whoever opens that seal now owns whatever happens next. I'm not saying no. I'm saying not here, not with Brannock at the gate and a landlady at the door."

He turns to Wenna, mild again. "Mistress, one more and we're gone. Did Jassan have visitors, or letters coming and going? Did he ever speak of anyone whose name starts *Serg*? Sergen, Sergio, a Sergeant somebody?"

Whatever she says, he wraps the stamp back up, reties the knot the way it was, and stows it inside his jerkin next to Vell's note. Then he sets the board back over the joists, the nails in their holes, and pushes the chair back onto it.

"Bram, you take the box. Sefa, walk beside him. I'll go out ahead and look at the street, and the gate post, before Brannock sees any of us with our arms full."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I take up a position just inside the doorway, keeping the landing in view without barring Wenna’s way.

“Leave the bundle wrapped until Sefa’s had a look. If that wax is magic, lead might be there for a reason.”

I study the green seal without touching it. “Vell described his own seal plainly. This isn’t it. We don’t carry it back pretending otherwise.”

Keeping my voice low, I add to my companions, “I’d like Brother Aldane’s opinion before we deliver anything—the drops, the death, and this seal, if he knows it. And Odda’s forty gold might be settled without stealing a page. First we find out whether that letter’s telling the truth.”

cards.title: Religion: whose mark are the scales over a closed eye?

presses.text:
I can’t press a card for that yet — no Religion card has come to me from the server; only the Arcana roll appeared. I’ll answer from what Sefa knows, and the DM can have me roll if more is needed.

On the sigil itself, not the magic in the wax: the scales over a shut eye is not a holy mark she was ever taught in the hospice. None of the gods of the Gate claim it — not Tymora’s coin, not the blind sword of Tyr’s justice, not Mask’s velvet half-mask. The nearest thing she can name is a moneylender’s private device, the sort a counting-house stamps on its own ledgers; older by far, the image of a blindfolded woman with scales and a sword is a symbol of law and judgment, but the eye is open in those, and the sword is absent here.

She thinks of seals not as holy signs but as bindings: a mark pressed into wax is a promise made bodily. The shut eye makes her think of someone signing for a bargain they won’t witness. “Scales and a shut eye: the old sign for a blind bargain — a debt weighed in the dark,” she says quietly.
presses.reply:
You're right to flag it, and thank you for doing it plainly. On my side both of Sefa's cards are waiting: Arcana for the living grain in the wax, and Religion for whose mark the scales over a shut eye might be. They come one after the other, so the Religion card should appear once the Arcana one is rolled. If it still doesn't show, tell me and I'll call it again.

What Sefa says aloud stands as her own words in the scene: "Scales and a shut eye: the old sign for a blind bargain, a debt weighed in the dark." The others will hear it as she says it.

What she actually recognises in the mark, or can rule out (which gods' signs it does or doesn't match, whether it's a holy symbol at all), is exactly what the Religion check is there to decide. I won't settle that from the reasoning above. I'll keep your read as Sefa's working guess, and once the die lands I'll narrate what her hospice schooling really gives her. That might confirm her guess, correct it, or leave it open. The same goes for the Arcana card and the grain in the wax.

If you'd rather Sefa not attempt the Religion check at all and just let her guess stand as a guess, say so and I'll withdraw that card. Otherwise, roll them in order when you're ready.

cards.title: Arcana: what is the living grain inside the green wax?

presses.text:
The green wax yields to her knowledge the way a fever yields to a steady hand. What looks like a trick of the light is not. The lines in the wax are real and deliberate: hair-fine threads of black glass caught in the wax and set in a spiral that coils inward to the shut eye. This is a seal meant to be broken once, by one whose name was spoken over it, and its closing isn't a lock — it's a witness. If it has been broken and recast, the join would fog at the edges where the wax meets the hasp, or the spiral would run off-true. It doesn't. The seal has never been opened since it was poured. And she knows what it cost, because that cost is written small: in the faint smudge of clean ash in the wax, in the way the wax holds a thumbprint that isn't Vell's, in the glass-threads that would cut the thumb of anyone who tried to lift it warm. A blood-price paid in silver and secrecy.

So the box is shut with magic that knows if it's been cut, and it was poured over Vell's lock by Jassan himself — or by someone who stood where Jassan stood and wanted this box preserved exactly as it is.

Sefa sees it plain: Vell's red-brown wax was already gone. Jassan didn't break a lock; he sealed over it, with a binding reserved for dead reckonings and last words. The seal isn't dangerous. It's a broken-truce marker — the kind of thing a man makes when he means to force a fair accounting and doesn't expect to be present when the box is opened.

And she is certain of one thing more. Such a seal doesn't hold against scrying. It attests. The strongbox itself is ordinary oak and iron; only the wax is warded, and only as a witness. The box can be opened, but the moment it is, whoever poured that wax — and anyone she can't name — may know it. That's not a trap in the base of the box. It's a notice that whatever is inside has waited three days for a particular pair of hands.

Now she reads the mark itself, the scales and the shut eye, and her memory does what it always did in the hospice: it sorts the candlelit faces of the gods into those she knows, and leaves one space where a face should be. No temple on the Steps carries that mark. The priestesses of Beshaba wear a broken wheel, not a scale. Hoar's weight of a winter hand is sometimes a scale, but always waking. Asmodeus' moneylenders stamp a balance and a flame. Not those. The shut eye is no god's sign. What the hospice sisters taught her, and what she's seen on ships' manifests and in old widows' boxes, is older and smaller: it's a witness-mark of blind account, the sort a notary might use in a city where law has failed — or a guild of record-keepers that locked their ledgers to their heads. Jassan wasn't calling a god. He was calling a record. And if the seal is whole, then night before last, when they carried Jassan out, whatever the barrel-chest promised was still true.

The smell of old paper in the room is old papier-mâché and dust. Not the sea. Not the grave.

Now, as the warmth ebbs from Pell's hands and the three of you turn to the landing, Wenna's answer about visitors comes dry and worn: "Two letters came for him in the last week of his life. One he burned in the grate, the one that left the curl. The other I never saw open. He had no visitors I know of, except the crooked-nosed man who came twice." Her arms are still folded. "Once the morning Jassan died, walking along the wall like he was admiring the building. And once today, with his purse."

Then the day's hush comes, the kind that sits in a town at its work. You hear the cooper's mallet rhythm fall once more, and a cart go by on the Coast Way.

Pell looks from the rewrapped stamp to the box and says, "The seal's been on here a while. The wax is clean where it meets the lock, so it hasn't been lifted. If the note Vell's seal was gone before this was put on, we're already carrying something different to what Vell thinks he hired us for." He tucks the little bundle away. "As for Odda Brand's page — I don't rip pages. But I'll count its paper and its corners, and if there's one loose in the binding, maybe that's Jassan's mistake, not ours." He says it without levity, like a man reciting a choice he hasn't finished making. "Vell might already know the widow. Or someone wants us to think he does."

What matters now is the order of sending. Bram thinks the box should go to Vell last, after you've had a chance to let its duplicates speak. He says there is no run now, but there may be one out the door, and he'll take the box if you two will read the street with him. He has a side-prong for the carrying. He looks to you, and then to the landing.

Then Wenna, looking down into the yard, says, "The crooked man is standing at the gate again, with a boy." Her voice is low. "The boy's pointing at the stairs."

Bram turns his head slowly to the doorway. Pell slides one hand inside his jerkin. The mallet stops mid-stroke. You hear the boy laugh, high and bright, out past the gate.

Pell says flatly, "Then we're not carrying it out the yard."

He looks to you. "You said you'd tell us when the seal would know. Can it tell if it's moved?" Then, to Bram: "If we go down the stair, Brannock sees the box." He doesn't finish the rest. He is already looking at the window, and the drop, and the street below.

presses.text:
The arcane threads in the wax resolve under Sefa's eye the way a fever-chart resolves under a steady hand. What she sees is not a ward, and not a lock. It's a dead man's reckon of sorrow, a witness with no mouth. She's seen its like only once, in a bundle brought to the hospice by a woman who never returned for it. In the dark of the sisters' linen-room, an old priest showed her how such a thing was made: not with fire, but with salt, and ash, and a spoken name.

But the box can be moved. It can be carried, hidden, set down in another room. The seal won't mind. What it will know is if someone opens it — not if someone carries it away. And here is the thing she holds in her mind now, cold and bright as the edge of a coin: that knowing may have already been spent. Such marks are made for a night, a vigil, a deadline. The one who poured it may have set a bound — dawn, or the miracle of a third day, or the reading of a will. Three days have passed since Jassan died. If the deadline was his own burial, it's already over. If it was dawn today, the seal may be spent in the open, reading only silence now. Sefa can't be certain which; the wax keeps its secret on the far side of its own breaking.

And the smell of old paper — she can state it flatly: not just that. Scrimshaw dust, thin and salt, hangs under it. It is the breath of a thing long kept dry by the sea, the unburned dust of a merchant's tally scratched on whalebone or shell. The wax holds specks of it. In that she feels a colder thread: scapular powder, ground mourning-shell, for marks made in salt. Nothing in this room was sealed by accident.

She looks at the empty chair and the cold grate. Jassan sealed that box with a mark of shame and account. A mark made, in the old custom, for a dead man. Then he sat down with it beside him and died in his chair.

Now, when she straightens, her voice is slow and even.

"It won't know if we move it," she says to Pell. "It will know if it's opened — or it would have known, if the one who poured it kept faith to hear. These marks are made for a fixed night, a vigil, a deadline." She looks down at the seal. "Three days is a long time for that kind of magic. It may already be deaf. But I wouldn't lift the lid in this room, in front of anyone, until we've decided what we mean to do." A pause. "And if I'm right, this isn't a lock. It's a funeral mark. A dead man's cotton and salt. Jassan sealed it as a reckoning, and then he died with it at his side."

She turns to Pell.

"You asked if it can tell if it's moved. It won't. So we can take it down the stairs with its seal intact, and the crooked man can watch all he likes. But first we owe ourselves a look at what he's doing at the gate. I'd rather serve Vell at noon than learn at the last that his rivals have run boys across the yard." She tucks her sleeves back, and the old hospice calm is on her face, cheerful and grim at once.

"And Bram's right to want Brother Aldane's testimony. Whatever killed Jassan, it was quiet, and it came while he kept a dead man's magic in his lap. That isn't a heart that stopped. That's a room that waited."

She steps to one side, giving the others a clear path to the box.

"Let's not keep the crooked-nosed man waiting the wrong kind of long."
presses.reply:
Thank you. That's a rich, careful read, and a good deal of it can come into play. Here's where it stands.

The Arcana die is cast, and the card is waiting for you to press Onward or ask for one of your allowed rerolls. Once you do, I'll narrate what Sefa actually makes of the grain in the green wax. After that her Religion card comes up for the scales over the shut eye. Until then I won't confirm or rule out any part of what you wrote about the seal: whether it's a ward, a witness or a funeral mark, whether it can tell it has been moved or opened, whether it's bound to a night or a deadline, or whether it has gone deaf. The scrimshaw dust and mourning-shell in the smell are the same. What the wax and the room really hold is the world's, and the dice decide how much of it she reads.
