Sefa Marrin: Sefa doesn’t answer Pell at once. She crosses to the strongbox, going down on one knee beside it with her hands folded, studying the green wax from less than a hand’s width away. Her lips move once, silently — not a prayer, the habit of reading a wound before touching it.

“The lines shift like ink running under glass, not like light,” she says at last, half to herself. “If it’s magic, it’s a maker’s mark, not a snare — but I wouldn’t warm it with a thumb.” She leans back a little, careful not to breathe on the seal. “Scales and a shut eye: the old dockside mark for a blind bargain, a debt weighed in the dark. Vell didn’t pour this. It was stamped here, I think, and in a hurry.” Her eyes move to the few crumbs of green wax beside the hole in the floor. “The same stuff by the joist.”

She gets to her feet, and her voice picks up its old hospice calm, the one she kept when a bedside went quiet. “Open the bundle here. If it’s lead, it’s hiding something from scrying — a key, a paper, a name. If it’s trapped, better a spirit hand finds the needle than yours.” Her eyes go to Pell. “I can lift it with a mage hand, turn the tied side toward the light and keep my fingers out of the dark. You watch the knot and the board. If it’s clean, you open it. If it isn’t, we set it down, close the boards, and carry better questions to Vell.”

She levels two fingers toward the wrapped bundle and speaks a word that is more breath than voice. A pale, spectral hand gathers in the air above it, thin as morning incense-smoke, and waits.

Then, for Wenna’s benefit as much as theirs, she adds quietly: “You said the room smelled of old paper. It smells of old secrets to me.”

Pell Dunmore: Pell weighs the bundle in his palm through the oilcloth a moment, then sets it down and speaks low to the other two.

"I'd bet my share that's a seal. Flat round face, neck, a knob to grip. Lead, so it's cheap and it's private. And green wax crumbs on the joist beside it." He nods at the box. "Jassan sealed that himself, his own mark, then hid the stamp under his own feet. Vell's wax was gone before we ever got here."

He works the clerk's knot loose with his fingertips, slowly, so it can be tied again the same way, and folds back the oilcloth without lifting what's inside. He looks at the face of it in the window light. Is it the scales and the shut eye? Is it cut backward, as a stamp should be? He sets it beside the box, near the green wax but not touching it, so all three can compare. He doesn't press it to anything.

"Sefa, the lines in that wax, the ones that move. Is that magic? A ward, a mark that tells someone if it's broken? I'd like to know what we're carrying before we carry it."

Then, quieter still, to Bram, about the letter:

"Your widow's page. Think on this before you decide anything. Jassan wrote to her, Jassan broke Vell's seal and put his own on, and Jassan burned something in that grate the night he died. We don't know the note's even still in there." A glance at the box. "And whoever opens that seal now owns whatever happens next. I'm not saying no. I'm saying not here, not with Brannock at the gate and a landlady at the door."

He turns to Wenna, mild again. "Mistress, one more and we're gone. Did Jassan have visitors, or letters coming and going? Did he ever speak of anyone whose name starts *Serg*? Sergen, Sergio, a Sergeant somebody?"

Whatever she says, he wraps the stamp back up, reties the knot the way it was, and stows it inside his jerkin next to Vell's note. Then he sets the board back over the joists, the nails in their holes, and pushes the chair back onto it.

"Bram, you take the box. Sefa, walk beside him. I'll go out ahead and look at the street, and the gate post, before Brannock sees any of us with our arms full."

Bram Halloway: I take up a position just inside the doorway, keeping the landing in view without barring Wenna’s way.

“Leave the bundle wrapped until Sefa’s had a look. If that wax is magic, lead might be there for a reason.”

I study the green seal without touching it. “Vell described his own seal plainly. This isn’t it. We don’t carry it back pretending otherwise.”

Keeping my voice low, I add to my companions, “I’d like Brother Aldane’s opinion before we deliver anything—the drops, the death, and this seal, if he knows it. And Odda’s forty gold might be settled without stealing a page. First we find out whether that letter’s telling the truth.”

scenes.narration:
Sefa goes down on one knee beside the strongbox, hands folded in her lap, and brings her face to within a hand's width of the green wax.

The grain is still there under the surface. It isn't light playing on the wax. It moves when nothing else does, slow lines turning over each other. Sefa watches it the way she used to watch a fever chart, without blinking, and this time she understands what she is looking at.

There is nothing in the wax that would bite. It isn't a ward and it isn't a curse. It's a keeping. Somebody bound it into the wax when it was poured, careful temple-work and very old, and the whole of the spell waits for one moment: when the wax breaks. Then it takes the likeness of the hand that broke it, and the face behind that hand, and holds them, the way a pressed flower holds its shape. The whorls are blank lines waiting to be written on. And the binding isn't closed. It runs out of the seal like a thread pulled taut toward something that isn't in this room, the way a lock is cut to answer one key. Whatever this seal records, it was made to be read somewhere else, by someone else. As the grain turns, a faint warmth gathers in her palms, the way a lamp-glass warms just before the wick is turned up, and then it's gone.

The mark itself won't come to her. She goes back over every shrine-corner and alms-box of the hospice wards and the Lower City temples where she ever lit a candle, and she can't find the scales with a shut eye beneath them anywhere. Weighers' guilds use scales, and so do half the counting-houses on the Coast. The eye means nothing to her. She says her own reading aloud: a blind bargain, stamped in haste, the same wax as the crumbs on the joist. Then she lifts two fingers. A pale, smoky hand gathers above the bundle and hangs there, waiting to be used.

Pell doesn't need it. He works the clerk's knot loose with his fingertips, one turn at a time, so he can tie it again the same way. Bram's voice comes from the doorway, telling him to leave it wrapped until Sefa has looked, while the second turn is already coming free. There is no needle in it and no powder in the folds. The oilcloth falls open on a squat lead stamp, the face dulled grey, the knob worn smooth by years of the same grip. Pell turns the face to the window. It shows scales over a closed eye, cut backwards and deep, the way a stamp should be cut, and it matches the seal on the box line for line. Round the thick neck runs a band of tiny letters in an old, cramped script. Pell can't read a word of it.

Sefa can. Writing has never stayed shut to her since the Lantern's book. *One hand of two. The other sees.* Close to the wax, she can feel the lead stamp too. It carries the same thin pull as the seal, the same thread leading out of the room.

Pell sets it on the boards beside the box, close to the green wax without touching it, and tells Bram in a low voice what he thinks of the widow's page: Jassan wrote to her, Jassan broke Vell's seal and laid his own, Jassan burned something the night he died, and whoever opens that box now owns whatever comes after. Then he turns to Wenna and asks her about visitors, letters, and anyone whose name begins *Serg*.

Wenna has been watching the smoky hand with her mouth pressed thin, and she doesn't take her eyes off it to answer. "Nobody came up to him. He went to Vell's mornings, came back nights. Letters, yes. He was a clerk. He wrote half the night some weeks. Tobin's boy ran them for a copper. Where they went you'd ask Tobin, I don't read the outsides of other people's post." She thinks about the rest. "Serg. The only Serg I know of is the sergeant at the Fist post on the Trade Way. Cowl. He's never been up my stair, and Jassan never named him to me." She glances at Sefa. "Old secrets. Then they're his, and you can carry them down my stair."

Pell wraps the stamp again, reties the knot the way it was, and puts it inside his jerkin beside Vell's note. He seats the board back over the joists and presses the nails home into their old holes with the heel of his hand, then sets the chair back on top of it. Wenna watches all of it and says nothing.

From the doorway, Bram looks down at the green seal a long while without touching it. He says plainly that Vell described his own seal, that this isn't it, and that they won't carry it back pretending otherwise. Then, low, he tells the other two that he wants Brother Aldane's word before anything is delivered: on the drops, on the death, and on this seal if the priest knows it. Odda's forty gold might be settled some way short of stealing a page, but first they need to know whether her letter tells the truth.

Pell steps past him onto the landing and looks down at the yard. The smoky hand above the floor thins and goes out.

Tobin is still at his hoop. The gate stands half open, and in the gap, right by the chalked post, a boy of nine or ten is squatting in the dust with a stick, drawing nothing in particular. Every so often he looks up at the stair. Beyond him the Coast Way smokes and rings. Two buildings back, toward the third smithy, a man in a leather jerkin sits on the farrier's mounting block with his forearms on his knees. He isn't holding a horse and he isn't waiting on one. He wasn't there when they came in.

Inside the room the strongbox sits by the chair where Jassan left it, its closed green eye turned up to the window light.

 Sefa tries once more to place the mark, scales over a closed eye, and she can't. Nothing from the hospice wards, the temple calendars or the alms-box carvings of the Lower City matches it, and she couldn't name for certain the god, guild or house it belongs to. Whose sign it is will have to come from someone else.

There is nothing in the wax that would bite. It isn't a ward and it isn't a curse. It's a keeping. Somebody bound it into the wax when it was poured, careful temple-work and very old, and the whole of the spell waits for one moment: when the wax breaks. Then it takes the likeness of the hand that broke it, and the face behind that hand, and holds them, the way a pressed flower holds its shape. The whorls are blank lines waiting to be written on. And the binding isn't closed. It runs out of the seal like a thread pulled taut toward something that isn't in this room, the way a lock is cut to answer one key. Whatever this seal records, it was made to be read somewhere else, by someone else. As the grain turns, a faint warmth gathers in her palms, the way a lamp-glass warms just before the wick is turned up, and then it's gone.

The mark itself won't come to her. She goes back over every shrine-corner and alms-box of the hospice wards and the Lower City temples where she ever lit a candle, and she can't find the scales with a shut eye beneath them anywhere. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays at the rail a moment, eyes idle, as if he's only judging the weather, and takes in the boy, the stick, the man on the mounting block. Then he steps back into the doorway and speaks low to Bram and Sefa.

"We're watched. A boy at the gate, playing lookout, and a man in a leather jerkin on the farrier's block who wasn't there when we came in. Brannock said he wouldn't be far. He meant it."

He thinks for half a breath.

"Bram's right about Aldane. The Song of the Morning is public, full of priests, and nobody jumps three people on a temple's steps. We take the box there first. Aldane looked at the body, he can look at the drops and the seal, and Sefa can talk to him in his own tongue. Then we carry it to Vell by daylight, down the middle of the Coast Way, with company. No alleys, no shortcuts." He glances at the strongbox. "And nobody opens it on the way. Not for Vell, not for Odda, not yet. Agreed?"

Before they lift anything, he goes down the stair. He steps over the pine tread, not on it, and crosses the yard to the cooper at his block. He keeps his back to the gate so the boy sees nothing but a hireling talking shop.

"Master Tobin. Mistress Pike says your boy ran Jassan's letters for a copper." He sets two coppers on the edge of the block. "Where did they go, these last weeks? Names, streets, a counting-house, the Fist post? And that lad squatting by your gate with the stick. Is he yours?"

If the boy isn't Tobin's, Pell asks one more thing, quieter: "Is there another way out of this yard? A back gate, a lane behind the stacks?"

He listens, nods his thanks, and keeps the man on the mounting block at the edge of his sight the whole time.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Before lifting the box, I snug my sword belt where I can reach it and settle my shield across my back.

“To the Song of the Morning first?” I ask Sefa and Pell quietly. “I want that seal left alone until we know more.”

I take the strongbox by its handles, keeping my fingers clear of the wax, and test its weight before starting down. I watch my footing at the raised tread.

In the yard I pause beside Tobin, keeping my voice low. “Mistress Pike says your boy carried Ferr’s letters. Is that him at the gate? I’d pay him for his time to tell us where he took them.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps to the doorway and puts only her head past the jamb, enough to read the yard and the street beyond without showing herself to the watchers. Then she draws back into the room and speaks low, first to Wenna.

“Mistress Pike. Is there a back way out of the yard — a lane gate behind the cooper’s shop, or a way through to the next street? There’s a boy at your gate and a man sitting between here and the third smithy with no horse and no business. We’d sooner carry a dead man’s box out the quiet way.”

Without waiting, she turns to Pell and Bram.

“The band around the stamp reads: *One hand of two. The other sees.*” She says it as if the words are still written on the air in front of her. “The seal and the stamp draw on the same thread, and it leads out of this room, not to us. The box can be moved, carried, shifted like any other oak; the wax keeps still. But if someone breaks that green seal, the spell will take the likeness of the hand that did it — and the face behind it — and keep it for the other hand to read.”

She lets that settle, then adds, quieter: “So we carry it whole, and we don’t let it be opened because some boy points or some man waits on a mounting block. If the back way is there, use it. If not, give me a breath and I can make the watchers look the wrong way while Bram takes the stair.”

scenes.narration:
Pell rests his forearms on the rail like a man checking the weather. He takes in the boy with the stick, the man on the mounting block, the empty stretch of road between them. Then he steps back into the doorway and tells the other two, low and quick, what he's seen and what he wants: the temple first, then Vell's by daylight down the middle of the Coast Way, and nobody opens the box.

Sefa leans her head past the jamb just long enough to see the same two figures, then draws back in and turns to Wenna.

Wenna doesn't have to think about it. "Tobin's timber gate. Back of the yard, behind the stave stacks. It's barred on the inside. It lets onto the muck lane behind the smithies, where the carts bring the oak in, and that comes out on the Trade Way by the horse trough." She looks at Sefa's hands, then at her face. "It's narrow, and the fences are high both sides. I'm only telling you what's there."

Sefa speaks to Pell and Bram while Pell is still at the door. She gives them the words on the stamp's neck, *One hand of two. The other sees*, and what the green wax is waiting for: the box can be carried and turned like any oak box, but whoever breaks the seal will leave their hand and face in it for the other hand to read. Then she offers to make the watchers look the wrong way if they need it.

Bram buckles his sword belt a notch tighter and swings the shield round onto his back. "To the Song of the Morning first? I want that seal left alone until we know more." He squats, takes the two iron handles and lifts. Vell didn't lie about the weight. It's a dead, settled heaviness, ledgers packed tight, and it pulls his arms straight before he gets it up against his chest with the green wax facing out and away from his fingers.

Pell is already on the stair. He steps over the pine tread and crosses the yard with his back to the gate, so the boy outside sees only a hireling talking shop with a cooper. He sets two coppers on the edge of the hooping block and asks his questions.

Tobin finishes the stroke he's on before he looks at the coins. "Not mine." He tips his bald head a fraction toward the gate. "Been sat there since you went up. Mine's round the back." He raises his voice without raising his eyes. "Dav!"

A boy of about twelve comes out from behind the steam box with his sleeves wet to the elbow, and Tobin flicks the two coppers across the block to him. "Tell him where you took the clerk's post. Then back to the staves."

Dav pockets the copper with the air of a man whose trade has been recognised. "Most of them went to Feldepost's, to the coach yard, for the Gate coach. Fat ones, every tenday or so. I can't read the outsides, but the coachman reads them out when he bags them. Gate, Lower City, and a name I never kept." He thinks. "One went to Mistress Brand's, off Tanner Lane, a tenday back. Never anything to the Fist." He scratches his wrist. "And the last night he gave me one at the stair foot, then took it back off me before I got to the gate. Said *not yet, Dav*. Didn't give me the copper, either."

Pell asks about another way out, and Tobin answers in four words, jerking his chin past the stacks. "Timber gate. Bar's inside."

Bram comes down the stair one tread at a time. The steps groan under him and the box. He feels for the raised pine tread with his boot, steps over it, and reaches the yard with the box still level against his chest. He stops beside Tobin and asks his own question. Dav answers it before the cooper can. "That's not me at the gate, master. I'm Dav. I just told him." Then his eyes go to the box in Bram's arms and he points at the green wax. "That's it. That's the same wax. All the Gate ones had that on."

Out by the post, the other boy has dropped his stick. He's on his feet the moment Bram comes off the stair, and he comes in through the half-open gate as far as the first barrel stack and no farther. It is the boy who pressed the letter into Bram's hand. He calls across the yard clearly enough for everyone to hear, Tobin and Dav and Wenna on the landing included.

"Master Halloway? The guard? Mistress Brand's on the bench at the chandler's. She says she'd like to see your face before you take that to Vell's. She says she won't keep you." He doesn't wait to be answered. He's back out through the gate and trotting up the Coast Way toward the town.

From the landing, Wenna watches him go. "Odda Brand's lad, that is," she says, to nobody in particular. "Harl's widow."

Two buildings back, the man on the farrier's mounting block has seen Bram on the stair with the box in his arms. He stands, stretches his back like a man with nowhere to be, and walks off up the Coast Way the same way the boy went: toward the chandler's bench, and toward Vell's. He doesn't hurry and he doesn't look round. The smoke from the third smithy closes behind his leather jerkin.

At the back of the yard, past the stave stacks, the timber gate stands shut with its bar across it. Tobin picks up his mallet and brings it down on the hoop.

 (Out of game) All three were played in the turn without a roll, because none of them was uncertain. Pell's talk and his questions to Tobin were plain conversation, and Tobin and Dav answered them. Bram set his belt and shield and carried the box down a stair he was watching, which is routine for a strong man taking care.

He thinks for half a breath.

"Bram's right about Aldane. The Song of the Morning is public, full of priests, and nobody jumps three people on a temple's steps. We take the box there first. Before they lift anything, he goes down the stair. He steps over the pine tread, not on it, and crosses the yard to the cooper at his block. He keeps his back to the gate so the boy sees nothing but a hireling talking shop.

"Master Tobin. Mistress Pike says your boy ran Jassan's letters for a copper." He sets two coppers on the edge of the block. "Where did they go, these last weeks? Names, streets, a counting-house, the Fist post? And that lad squatting by your gate with the stick. Is he yours?"

If the boy isn't Tobin's, Pell asks one more thing, quieter: "Is there another way out of this yard? A back gate, a lane behind the stacks?"

messages.text:
“Thank you, Dav.”

I turn to Sefa and Pell. “I’ll speak with Odda. She’s waiting in public, and I won’t lead that man into a narrow lane with this in my arms. Keep close, please.”

I carry the box out through the front gate, leaving the wax untouched, and head toward the chandler’s along the open street. I watch for the leather jerkin rather than following him blindly into the smithy smoke.

If we reach Odda without interruption, I stop beside her bench.

“Mistress Brand? I have your letter. Tell me about Harl’s debt—and what Jassan told you. We haven’t opened the box.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell flicks Dav one more copper before the boy can get back to his staves.

"That name the coachman read out on the fat letters, Dav. Think hard. Did it start like *Serg*? Sergen, Sergeant, anything near it? And did the Gate letters ever come back here, replies with green wax on them?"

Whatever Dav says, Pell nods his thanks and steps over beside Bram and Sefa, voice low.

"So Jassan was sealing his letters to someone in the Gate with that stamp, and he put the same seal on Vell's box. 'One hand of two, the other sees.' Whoever breaks that wax gets their face shown to Jassan's friend in the Gate. Vell, Odda, us." He touches his jerkin where the stamp sits. "And we're carrying the other hand. That's worth something to somebody. Keep it quiet."

He glances at the timber gate, then away from it.

"Not the back lane. High fences both sides, Bram's arms full, and Brannock already said 'long way down the Coast Way'. That's where I'd wait if I were him. We go out the front, in the open. Odda's bench is on our road anyway. Bram, she asked for you, so you hear her out. But in daylight, on the bench, box on your knees, and nobody decides anything there. Then the temple, then Vell."

To Sefa: "If the jerkin's waiting near that bench, keep your trick ready. Use it only if somebody moves for the box."

Then he goes ahead of them through the front gate. He doesn't glance at the chalk this time. He walks loose and easy up the Coast Way a dozen paces ahead of Bram, keeping to the side where the smithy smoke and the carts give him cover. He watches for the leather jerkin, for Brannock's grey head, and for anyone falling in behind once Bram comes out with the box. When the chandler's bench comes in sight, he stops short of it, finds a wall to lean on where he can see Odda, the bench and both ends of the street, and lets Bram walk past him to her.

scenes.narration:
Bram shifts the box against his chest to get a better grip. "Thank you, Dav." He turns to the other two. "I'll speak with Odda. She's waiting in public, and I won't lead that man into a narrow lane with this in my arms. Keep close, please."

Before Dav can get back behind the steam box, a copper spins through the air and he catches it against his wet sleeve. Pell asks his two questions. Dav frowns at the coin as if the answer might be written on it.

"Not Serg. If it was a sergeant the coachman would've said *sergeant*, he likes a title, him." He screws up his face. "He said *care of*. 'Gate, Lower City, care of' and then the name. I remember the *care of* because he laughed at it, like it was a fine way to write." He thinks about the second question and shakes his head. "Came back? Not to me. Master Ferr went down to Feldepost's himself, some evenings when the coach was in. If anything came back for him, he fetched it." Then he's gone behind the steam box. Tobin's mallet comes down on the hoop.

Pell steps in close to the other two and says his piece in a low voice: Jassan sealed his Gate letters and Vell's box with the same stamp, the twin hand at the other end sees whoever breaks it, and the other half of the pair is sitting in his jerkin. They go out by the front, in the open, and nobody decides anything at the bench. He glances once at the timber gate and away again. Then he's through the front gate ahead of them, not looking at the chalk, loose-shouldered, one more hireling on the Coast Way.

Bram follows with the box held level against his mail and the green wax turned outward, away from his hands. Sefa keeps pace at his shoulder. On the road the weight shows. A carter swings wide around them, and an apprentice with an armful of tongs stops to stare at the iron-cornered box until his master shouts at him. Bram walks down the middle of the street where the carts have packed it hard. He doesn't hurry and he doesn't go into the smoke after anyone.

Pell stays a dozen paces ahead on the smithy side, where the carts and smoke hide him. Reading a street is work he's done since he was twelve, and he does it without a pause. The jerkin is easy to find. The man is well past the chandler's, near the bend where Vell's end of the street begins, leaning on the post of an alehouse doorway with a cup he isn't drinking from. A second man stands beside him, thick through the shoulders, in a carter's smock that doesn't fit, with a hand on the doorframe. Neither of them moves toward the bench. They watch the road the way men watch for a cart they've been told is coming. Nobody falls in behind Bram. Pell picks a stretch of wall by the chandler's shutters where he can see the bench, the alehouse door and the way back to the yard. He leans on it and lets Bram go past.

- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa closes the distance, keeping Bram between her and the street. To Odda she speaks low, not unkind.

“We won’t break it open at a bench, mistress — and I won’t put my hand in a dead man’s ledger on hearsay, not yours, not Vell’s. But you’ll have a witness.” She nods once toward the box. “When it reaches the counter, I mean to tell Vell the box was sealed with Jassan’s own mark when we found it, not his, and ask him to count his pages where we can see. If Harl’s note is still there, we’ll hold the man to honest tally. If it’s gone, that’s Jassan’s hand, not ours — and not yours.”

She straightens, her voice turning practical.

“The grey-haired man just left the alehouse with two shadows, and he means to stand between us and Vell’s door. I don’t care to be herded.” She catches Pell’s eye. “Let’s not go straight down his throat along the Way. Up the street to the Song of the Morning instead — in daylight, in the open. The temple owes Master Vell a second look at this box, and it gives us a porch where no one can take it off Bram without a public scene.”

She falls in beside Bram, a half-step to his right, close enough to block a reach from the street side.

“Once we’re off the road and under temple eaves, someone should walk the rail and see if those two follow past the turn. If they do, we know.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell gives it a slow count of ten against the wall, watching Coll settle in at the alehouse. Then he pushes off and drifts over to the bench like a man joining his friend. He stops at Bram's shoulder, half-turned, so he can still see the alehouse door past the chandler's sign.

He keeps his voice low and kind, for Odda.

"Mistress Brand. I'm with him. Nobody's opening anything on this street, and nobody's deciding anything here. But I want to understand you right." He nods at the paper in her hand. "That's Jassan's letter? Why would Vell's own clerk warn you? Did you know him? Did he owe Harl something, or say why he'd turned on his master?" A beat. "And did he name anyone else in it? Someone in the Gate, or Dobbin, or a man called Thale?"

He listens, watching her hands and her face more than her words.

Then, still quiet, to Bram and Sefa: "Brannock and his two are on the alehouse step, square between us and Vell's door. They're not coming to us. They're waiting for us to come to them." He glances at Odda again. "Mistress, which way to the Song of the Morning from here? Is there a road that doesn't run past the Juggler's end of the street? A wide one, with people on it."

If there's a good road, he means to take it. He'll go ahead as before, Bram and the box in the middle of the street, Sefa at his shoulder. Before he leaves the bench he tells Odda plainly: "We'll come find you before this is finished, one way or the other. I won't promise more than that."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Forty gold borrowed—is forty still the whole sum he claims? And is the house pledged in writing?”

I shift my grip on the handles.

“I believe you about Jassan’s warning. But tearing out a page may not clear the debt, and I won’t promise your roof on a guess. There may be another way to settle it.”

I glance toward Coll and his two companions, then back to Odda.

“Keep both letters safe. We’re going to the Song of the Morning before we go near Vell. If someone presses you about us, you needn’t answer.”

To Sefa and Pell, quietly: “Three men waiting now. Let’s turn toward the temple while there’s still room. If they approach, I’ll set this down before we talk.”

scenes.narration:
Sefa moves in close to the bench and keeps Bram's bulk between herself and the street. She talks to Odda in a low voice. Nobody breaks anything open at a bench. She won't put her hand in a dead man's ledger on anyone's word. When the box reaches Vell's counter she means to tell him whose mark was on it and ask him to count his pages where they can all see. If Harl's note is gone, that was Jassan's doing and not Odda's.

Odda hears her out. "It won't be gone, mistress. He wrote that he couldn't unwrite it." She doesn't sound angry about it. "Counting won't help me if it's there."

Pell gives the alehouse a slow count of ten from his wall. Then he pushes off and wanders over to the bench like a man coming to join a friend, and stops at Bram's shoulder half-turned, so the chandler's sign doesn't block his view of Coll's doorway. He asks his questions gently. Bram asks his over the top of the box. Odda takes them in the order they came. She keeps her hands still on the folded letter, and her face doesn't change between one answer and the next. Pell has watched a great many people tell him things, and there's nothing in her to read except tiredness.

"I washed for him. Shirts and collars, every tenday, a copper a shirt. That's how I knew him." She turns her red hands over a little, as if they explained it. "He didn't owe Harl anything. He was civil. He'd ask after the boy. The last time he brought his washing he asked whether Harl had ever talked about a cloth merchant. I said Harl talked about mules. He didn't say why he asked." She looks down at the letter. "He named nobody in this. You read all of it. Dobbin I know from Harl. Thale I know of: a lender up the Trade Way. Harl wouldn't go to him. He said Thale's terms were worse than Vell's."

To Bram: "Forty borrowed. Forty-six owed by midsummer, with the interest. That was written on the note too." She keeps her voice level. "And the house. Harl put it down as his surety. I watched him sign it, and I didn't stop him. We needed the mules."

Bram tells her what he believes and what he won't promise. Tearing a page out might not clear the debt, and there may be another way to settle it. He asks her to keep the letters safe, and tells her they're going to the temple before they go anywhere near Vell. If anyone asks her about them, she doesn't have to answer.

Odda nods once, slowly, like a woman who expected less and is taking what she was given without counting it. "I've only the one letter, Master Halloway. You have the other." She tucks Jassan's paper back inside her shawl.

Pell asks the way to the Song of the Morning, a road that stays clear of the Juggler's end and has people on it. She points back the way they came, past the cooper's yard. "Down the Coast Way to the horse trough, where it meets the Trade Way. Then south. The temple's on the rise, outside the houses, you'll see the gilt on the roof. The Juggler's up the other end, by the Fist post." Pell tells her plainly that they'll come and find her before this is finished, one way or the other, and that he won't promise more than that. "That's more than I had this morning," she says. She gets up, calls the boy off the end of the plank, and the two of them go off up a side alley toward Tanner Lane without looking back at the box.

They go back the way they came. Pell walks a dozen paces ahead on the smithy side. Bram keeps to the hard-packed middle of the street with the box against his chest. Sefa stays half a step off his right shoulder, on the street side, close enough to block a reaching hand. They pass the cooper's yard. The chalk mark is still on the post, and Tobin's mallet is still going. Pell looks back once, between a cart and a quench-tub, and there's no need for anyone to walk the rail to find out. Coll Brannock has stepped down off the alehouse step. He's walking down the Coast Way after them at an easy stroll with his hands loose at his sides, and the jerkin man and the man in the badly fitting smock are a pace behind him on either side. They don't close the gap and they don't let it grow. Through the whole length of the street, past the farrier's and the third smithy, they stay about forty feet back.

The Coast Way runs out at a long stone horse trough green with slime, where it meets the Trade Way. The big road is busy: an ox-wagon of charcoal, two drovers with a string of mules, a pedlar's handcart, a pair of Lathander's lay brothers in rose-coloured tabards walking south with baskets. Down the road, beyond the last roofs, a gilt ridge catches the sun on a low rise, a long quarter-mile off.

Behind them Coll stops beside the trough, thirty feet back, and his two men spread out a little, one toward each verge. He folds his hands over his belt next to the cudgel and lets a mule string pass between them.

"Temple first. Careful people, like I said." His voice carries easily, and there's nothing hard in it. "I'll walk with you as far as the steps, friend. It's a fine morning for it, and my man's offer keeps better than Vell's."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets the mule string pass and doesn't hurry. He gives Bram and Sefa a small nod, *keep walking*, and steers them so their road south runs right beside the two lay brothers in rose tabards. He gives the brothers a friendly "Morning, brothers. Going up to the Song? So are we," and falls in step near them. Company in Lathander's colours is the best escort on the Trade Way.

Then he drops back half a pace, enough that Coll can come alongside him without getting anywhere near Bram and the box. He speaks easy, the dockside vowels coming out to meet Coll's own.

"Walk with us, then. It's a public road." He keeps his hands loose and in sight. "But if your man's offer keeps so well, let's hear it out loud instead of having it follow us. Who is he? Thale? And what's he paying, and for what? The box, or what's in it?"

A beat, then lower, in the roof cadence again: *"The wax isn't the colour you were told."* He watches Coll's face for whether that's news.

"I'll tell you plain how it stands. We were hired to carry it, and we'll carry it. Nobody's opening it on the road, not for you, not for us. So if your man wants to read Vell's books, he'll have to do better than walk us to a temple." He tilts his head, curious rather than hostile. "Unless he's after something else Jassan had. Did your man ever trade letters with a clerk? Someone in the Gate, maybe?"

He keeps one eye on the jerkin man and the smock on the verges the whole way. If either of them drifts in toward Bram, Pell stops walking and says, still pleasant: "Your friends are crowding the brothers, Coll. Call them off, or we have this talk on the temple steps with every priest listening."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I keep walking toward the temple at a steady pace, staying on the travelled road.

“You can make an offer without following at our heels, Master Brannock,” I call back. “Name your employer and your terms. You’ll get no agreement on the road.”

Quietly, to Sefa: “Watch the one on your side. If they close in, I’m putting the box down. I won’t fight with it in my arms.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn’t break stride. She puts one hand briefly on Bram’s arm, not to slow him, just enough to make sure he keeps moving, and speaks low and calm. “Don’t set it down. If they want the box, they take it off two of us in broad daylight, not one.”

Then she shifts half a step so she’s between Brannock’s approach and the man with the box, and raises her voice just enough for it to travel across the space he’s been careful to keep.

“Your man’s offer can wait for the steps, Master Brannock. I don’t barter on the Trade Way with three men spread at a dead man’s back.” She lifts one hand, palm out, to mark the thirty-foot distance he’s been keeping, as if it were a line he’d chosen. “Tell your pair to keep their thumbs where I can see them and their feet on the road. We’ll hear you at the temple, but it’ll be the four of us and whatever gods are watching, not an ambush with a handcart for cover.”

She doesn’t turn fully away from him, walking sideways enough to keep him and his men in sight. “And if your master has a name, now’s a fair time for it. I’d hate to find out he answers to Gerrit Thale by his men closing in at the steps.”

scenes.narration:
Pell lets the mule string pass and doesn't hurry. He gives Bram and Sefa a small nod, *keep walking*, and steers the three of them out onto the Trade Way just as the two lay brothers in rose tabards come level with the trough. Each brother has a covered basket on his arm, and the smell of new bread drifts out from under the cloths.

"Morning, brothers. Going up to the Song? So are we."

The older one has a sunburnt scalp and a face that smiles easily. He looks at Bram's mail, at the iron-cornered box against his chest, and past them at the three men by the trough. His smile stays on, but it gets more careful. "We are, and you're welcome to the road. Rolls for the almshouse." He shifts his basket to the other arm so the box can pass on the crown of the road. "Your friends behind are welcome too, if they keep a civil step."

The company moves off south with rose tabards on its left. Pell drops half a pace behind and to the side, so anyone who wants to come up beside him has to do it well clear of Bram. Coll takes the hint. He leaves the trough at the same easy stroll and closes until he's walking at Pell's elbow, hands loose at his sides. The jerkin man and the man in the smock stay on the verges, one on each side, as far back as they were.

Pell speaks to him in dockside vowels to match his own. It's a public road. If the offer keeps so well, let's hear it out loud. Who is he, Thale? What's he paying, and for what: the box, or what's in it? Then, lower, in the up-and-down rhythm of the roofs: *"The wax isn't the colour you were told."*

Coll doesn't look surprised. He doesn't pretend to be, either. He answers in the same rhythm, quietly enough that the brothers hear only two men muttering: "Hinges have gaps, friend." On the roofs that means *I've already seen it.* Then, in plain speech: "Not the colour he told you. You noticed that. That's worth something, and it's worth more to my man than it is to yours."

Ahead, Bram keeps the same steady pace down the travelled middle of the road and calls back over the box without turning his head. "You can make an offer without following at our heels, Master Brannock. Name your employer and your terms. You'll get no agreement on the road." Then, low, to Sefa: "Watch the one on your side. If they close in, I'm putting the box down. I won't fight with it in my arms."

Sefa doesn't break stride. She lays a hand on his arm for a moment, not to hold him back, just to keep him walking. "Don't set it down. If they want the box, they'll have to take it off two of us in broad daylight, not one." Then she steps half a pace across, so her body is between Coll's side of the road and the box, and raises her voice just enough to carry. She won't barter on the Trade Way with three men spread out at a dead man's back. She lifts one palm toward the gap the verge men have kept, as if it were a line they drew themselves. Their thumbs stay in sight and their feet stay on the road. And if their master has a name, now is a fair time for it, before she finds out he answers to Gerrit Thale by his men closing in at the steps. She walks half sideways to keep the three of them in view.

Coll looks at her for the first time since the trough. He seems pleased, like a man watching someone else play a hand well. He lifts two fingers from his belt and lowers them. On the left verge the jerkin man has drifted a step toward the brothers. He stops and lets the gap open again. The smock man never moved.

"You've a good memory for names, mistress. Vell gave you that one, I expect. Vell isn't wrong about everything." It's as close as he comes to saying yes. Then he answers Bram, and he says it to all three of them at a pleasant, even pitch the brothers can hear too, because he has nothing in it to hide. "Terms, then. Eighty gold for the box as it stands, unopened, wax whole, whatever colour it is. That beats seventy-five, and it's paid when the box changes hands, not when somebody's satisfied." He walks a few steps. "A hundred and twenty if the three of you carry it to my man yourselves and tell him, in your own words, where you found it and whose seal was on it. Vell's own bearers saying so are worth forty gold to him." He gives Pell a sidelong look. "My man doesn't want it opened on the road any more than you do, friend. He reads ledgers. He doesn't break them."

Pell has one more question: did his man ever trade letters with a clerk, maybe someone in the Gate? Coll takes a moment over it. Pell can see him put the thought somewhere and keep it. "My man doesn't write north. Everything he wants is on this road." A pause. "Letters to the Gate, though. Your clerk had a busy hand."

The road starts to rise. The last roofs of Beregost fall behind, and the Song of the Morning stands up ahead on its low hill: pale stone, rose-coloured doors open on a shaded porch, the gilt ridge burning in the sun. A dozen broad, shallow steps climb to the porch, worn hollow in the middle. A woman in rose robes is sweeping them. An old man sits on the top step with a crutch across his knees, waiting for the almshouse rolls.

At the bottom step Coll stops. His two men stop on the verges behind him.

"I'll be here," he says, looking up at the open doors. "Eighty, or a hundred and twenty. Nobody in there will raise it." He folds his hands over his belt beside the cudgel. "And every road out of this temple runs past these steps, friend. That isn't a threat. It's just how it's built."

The brothers go up past the sweeping woman with their baskets. The old man on the top step lifts the cloth off one of them, and the smell of warm bread spills down the steps. Bram stands at the foot of them with the box in his arms and the green seal facing the morning.

Coll doesn't look surprised. He doesn't pretend to be, either. He answers in the same rhythm, quietly enough that the brothers hear only two men muttering: "Hinges have gaps, friend." On the roofs that means *I've already seen it.* Then, in plain speech: "Not the colour he told you. You noticed that. That's worth something, and it's worth more to my man than it is to yours."

Ahead, Bram keeps the same steady pace down the travelled middle of the road and calls back over the box without turning his head. "You can make an offer without following at our heels, Master Brannock. Name your employer and your terms. You'll get no agreement on the road." Then, low, to Sefa: "Watch the one on your side. Sefa doesn't break stride. She lays a hand on his arm for a moment, not to hold him back, just to keep him walking. "Don't set it down. If they want the box, they'll have to take it off two of us in broad daylight, not one." She won't barter on the Trade Way with three men spread out at a dead man's back. She lifts one palm toward the gap the verge men have kept, as if it were a line they drew themselves. Their thumbs stay in sight and their feet stay on the road. And if their master has a name, now is a fair time for it, before she finds out he answers to Gerrit Thale by his men closing in at the steps. She walks half sideways to keep the three of them in view.

Coll looks at her for the first time since the trough. He seems pleased, like a man watching someone else play a hand well. He lifts two fingers from his belt and lowers them. On the left verge the jerkin man has drifted a step toward the brothers. He stops and lets the gap open again. The smock man never moved.

"You've a good memory for names, mistress. Vell gave you that one, I expect. Vell isn't wrong about everything." It's as close as he comes to saying yes. Then he answers Bram, and he says it to all three of them at a pleasant, even pitch the brothers can hear too, because he has nothing in it to hide. "Terms, then. Eighty gold for the box as it stands, unopened, wax whole, whatever colour it is. That beats seventy-five, and it's paid when the box changes hands, not when somebody's satisfied." He walks a few steps. "A hundred and twenty if the three of you carry it to my man yourselves and tell him, in your own words, where you found it and whose seal was on it. He doesn't break them."

"My man doesn't write north. Everything he wants is on this road." A pause. "Letters to the Gate, though. Your clerk had a busy hand."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Then you’ll have no trouble finding us when we’re ready to answer.”

I climb the steps with Sefa and Pell, giving the old man and his crutch room to pass. To the woman sweeping, I say, “Good morning. We’re looking for Brother Aldane, who examined Jassan Ferr. We’ve questions about his death, and a sealed box from his room. Is there somewhere we can speak privately?”

Once we’re inside and clear of the doorway, I lower the strongbox carefully to the floor, keeping the seal untouched, and bring my shield back onto my arm.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her place half a step ahead of Bram, so that the first body up the temple steps is hers, not the box’s. She doesn’t run from Brannock’s patience; she lets it hang behind them while the sound of the broom on stone sets the pace.

When she reaches the bottom step, she pauses just long enough for the old man and the woman to mark their faces, then says to Pell and Bram, low: “Get it onto the porch, into the shade. I want Brother Aldane. He was the one who looked at Jassan; he’ll know whether the room was still holy when he got there, and whose funeral wax that is.”

She starts up, then turns on the third step, looking down at Coll without heat.

“Your offer’s been heard, and it’ll keep at the foot of the hill as well as it did at the trough. But the temple steps aren’t a market, Master Brannock. Leave your cudgel-men off the stone, and we’ll come down with an answer when there is one.”

Then she turns her back on him, climbs the rest of the way, and steps into the shaded porch where the smell of new bread and cool stone settles over the morning like a clean cloth.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops on the bottom step, turns, and gives Coll a short, easy nod, the kind one dock rat gives another.

"Eighty or a hundred and twenty. I heard you. Enjoy the sun." Then, roof cadence, light: *"Long wait on a short step."* Meaning *we'll come out when we come out, and not a moment before.*

He goes up past the sweeping woman, keeping half a step behind Bram so his own back is between the box and the road. At the top he stops for the old man with the crutch and drops two coppers in the basket's cloth. "For the bread, father." To the woman with the broom, polite and quiet:

"Sister, we're looking for Brother Aldane. He looked at a dead man three days ago, a clerk named Jassan Ferr, above the cooper's yard. We've something of the clerk's he ought to see. Is he in?"

Once they're inside, out of sight of the steps, he speaks low to Bram and Sefa before anyone comes:

"Box stays in your arms, Bram, or at your feet with your boot against it. Nobody here touches the wax either, not even a priest with good intentions. We show it, we don't hand it over." He touches his jerkin. "The stamp stays where it is unless I say. Coll knows about the colour. He doesn't know we've got the other hand, and I'd like to keep it that way."

When Aldane comes, Pell lets Sefa do the greeting. Then he takes the cloth-wrapped vial from the satchel and holds it out, cork in.

"Brother. Jassan took three drops of this every night, he said for his chest. His landlady found the bottle knocked over by his foot. Bitter, green, like leaves steeped in spirit. What is it? What does too much of it do? And when you looked at him: lips, nails, eyes, anything that didn't sit right with a plain failed heart?"

He waits for the answer, then adds one more:

"And who in Beregost sells a thing like this? Apothecary, herb-wife, someone off the caravans?"

scenes.narration:
Coll doesn't move from the foot of the steps. When Bram tells him they'll be easy to find, he only tips his head, like a man agreeing about the weather.

Sefa goes up first, half a step ahead of the box. On the third step she turns and speaks down to him without heat. Coll hears her out. Then he takes one pace back off the bottom step onto the packed dust of the road, and behind him the jerkin man and the smock man ease back onto the verges.

"Off the stone, mistress." He settles his hands on his belt. "I've no quarrel with the Morninglord."

Pell gives him a short dock-rat nod from the bottom step. *"Long wait on a short step."*

Coll answers in the same rise and fall, quietly enough that the broom covers it. *"Sun's long today, friend."* On the roofs that means *I can wait as long as you can.* He doesn't look at the doors again. He looks at the road, the way a man watches the only way out of a yard.

At the top the old man with the crutch has a roll in each hand. When Pell drops two coppers into the cloth over the basket he looks up, surprised. "Dawn keep you, lad." He goes back to the bread.

The sister with the broom is young and freckled, and the hem of her rose robe is grey with step-dust. She hears Bram's question and then Pell's, and looks from the mail to the iron-cornered box to the green wax. "Brother Aldane's in the infirmary. He keeps the sick-room. Come through, and don't mind the novices. They stare at anyone in armour." She leans the broom against a pillar and leads them in.

The nave is cool and smells of beeswax and lime. A tall east window of rose and amber glass throws a smear of warm colour across the floor, and a handful of townsfolk kneel in it with their eyes shut. Nobody looks up at the box. The sister takes them down a side passage, past a door where two novices are folding bandages and stop to watch Bram go by, and into a long whitewashed room with six cots, four of them empty. Shelves of stoppered jars climb one wall. An old woman sleeps in the end cot with her mouth open. The window over the worktable looks south onto the herb beds. The road and the steps can't be seen from here.

"Brother, people for you. About the clerk." The sister goes back to her broom.

Bram finds a clear stretch of floor by the worktable and lowers the box slowly, the green wax facing up and away from everyone's hands. He straightens, swings the shield off his back and onto his arm, and stands with one boot against the oak. While the sister's steps fade down the passage, Pell gives the other two his piece in a low voice: show it, don't hand it over, and the stamp stays where it is.

Brother Aldane is grinding something at the worktable, and he finishes the turn of the pestle before he puts it down. He's past sixty, broad, with big clean hands and short white hair. He wears a rose stole over a linen apron stained green-brown at the front. He wipes his hands on a cloth and looks the three of them over, the box last.

Sefa greets him. Then Pell unwraps the vial from its cloth and holds it out, cork in, and asks his questions one after another.

Aldane doesn't take the vial. He doesn't need to. "That's mine. Foxglove, steeped in spirit. I made it up for him at the thaw, when he came in with his heart stumbling on the stairs." He holds up three thick fingers. "Three drops in water, at night. It steadies a weak heart and slows a fast one. Too much and you're sick first. You vomit, you see a yellow ring round every candle, and your heart goes wrong in a way you feel. There was no sick on him, on the floor or in the basin. A finger left in that bottle is about right for a month's use. He didn't take too much, and nobody gave him any."

He answers the rest in the same plain order. "His lips were grey-blue and his nails the same, and his hands were cold to the wrist. That's what a heart that stops does to a man. His eyes were open, and Wenna had closed them by the time I came. There was no smell on him but the drops and old paper. No marks on his throat, his wrists or anywhere else. I looked, because Vell paid for the burial and I wanted to know what I was putting my name to." He nods at the vial. "And who sells it? Nobody. I make it for this infirmary. The herb-wives won't touch foxglove, and they're right not to. I wouldn't trust it from a caravan."

Sefa asks about the room and the wax. He gives her a short look, and there's something gentler in it than in his answers to Pell. "I said the dawn words over him in his chair. The room was a room, mistress. A man died in it, and that doesn't foul a place." Then he lowers himself onto one knee beside the box with a grunt, sets one hand flat on the floor to keep his weight off it, and looks at the seal from a forearm's length without touching it.

He stays there a while.

"That's not funeral wax. I don't know of any." His finger hovers over the scales and doesn't come down. "Those are the Merchantfriend's. Waukeen's, the old way of drawing them. My father kept a bond from her house in the Gate, from before she went quiet in the Troubles. It had green wax like this and scales on it. He wouldn't let us children near it." He looks a moment longer at the closed eye under the beam, and his mouth tightens. "The eye wasn't on his. I've never seen that."

He gets up slowly, one hand on the table edge, and wipes his palms on the cloth again though they're clean.

"He was here the day before he died. Not for his drops. He sat in the second pew from the noon bell until the light went off the east window, and then he came back here and asked me something I've thought about every day since." Aldane folds the cloth in half and lays it on the table. "I'll tell you what he asked. First tell me why three armed people bring a dead clerk's box to a temple instead of to Ostrin Vell, with a man and two bruisers waiting at the bottom of my steps. The sister saw them, and so did I, from the porch."

In the end cot the old woman sighs in her sleep and turns toward the wall. Outside the window a bee works its way along the sage. On the floor the green wax holds the light from the herb beds, the scales and the closed eye turned up toward the whitewashed ceiling.

 (Out of game) None of the four needed a roll, and all of them happened in the turn: these were plain words and ordinary movement with nothing uncertain in them. Sefa did say aloud to get the box into the shade, but Bram's own declared action was to carry it inside and set it on the floor, so it ended up in the infirmary.

relay.request:
Characters at the table: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.
In this scene: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.
Write the screens of, in this order: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Bram Halloway: “Then you’ll have no trouble finding us when we’re ready to answer.”

I climb the steps with Sefa and Pell, giving the old man and his crutch room to pass. To the woman sweeping, I say, “Good morning. We’re looking for Brother Aldane, who examined Jassan Ferr. We’ve questions about his death, and a sealed box from his room. Is there somewhere we can speak privately?”

Once we’re inside and clear of the doorway, I lower the strongbox carefully to the floor, keeping the seal untouched, and bring my shield back onto my arm.

Sefa Marrin: Sefa keeps her place half a step ahead of Bram, so that the first body up the temple steps is hers, not the box’s. She doesn’t run from Brannock’s patience; she lets it hang behind them while the sound of the broom on stone sets the pace.

When she reaches the bottom step, she pauses just long enough for the old man and the woman to mark their faces, then says to Pell and Bram, low: “Get it onto the porch, into the shade. I want Brother Aldane. He was the one who looked at Jassan; he’ll know whether the room was still holy when he got there, and whose funeral wax that is.”

She starts up, then turns on the third step, looking down at Coll without heat.

“Your offer’s been heard, and it’ll keep at the foot of the hill as well as it did at the trough. But the temple steps aren’t a market, Master Brannock. Leave your cudgel-men off the stone, and we’ll come down with an answer when there is one.”

Then she turns her back on him, climbs the rest of the way, and steps into the shaded porch where the smell of new bread and cool stone settles over the morning like a clean cloth.

Pell Dunmore: Pell stops on the bottom step, turns, and gives Coll a short, easy nod, the kind one dock rat gives another.

"Eighty or a hundred and twenty. I heard you. Enjoy the sun." Then, roof cadence, light: *"Long wait on a short step."* Meaning *we'll come out when we come out, and not a moment before.*

He goes up past the sweeping woman, keeping half a step behind Bram so his own back is between the box and the road. At the top he stops for the old man with the crutch and drops two coppers in the basket's cloth. "For the bread, father." To the woman with the broom, polite and quiet:

"Sister, we're looking for Brother Aldane. He looked at a dead man three days ago, a clerk named Jassan Ferr, above the cooper's yard. We've something of the clerk's he ought to see. Is he in?"

Once they're inside, out of sight of the steps, he speaks low to Bram and Sefa before anyone comes:

"Box stays in your arms, Bram, or at your feet with your boot against it. Nobody here touches the wax either, not even a priest with good intentions. We show it, we don't hand it over." He touches his jerkin. "The stamp stays where it is unless I say. Coll knows about the colour. He doesn't know we've got the other hand, and I'd like to keep it that way."

When Aldane comes, Pell lets Sefa do the greeting. Then he takes the cloth-wrapped vial from the satchel and holds it out, cork in.

"Brother. Jassan took three drops of this every night, he said for his chest. His landlady found the bottle knocked over by his foot. Bitter, green, like leaves steeped in spirit. What is it? What does too much of it do? And when you looked at him: lips, nails, eyes, anything that didn't sit right with a plain failed heart?"

He waits for the answer, then adds one more:

"And who in Beregost sells a thing like this? Apothecary, herb-wife, someone off the caravans?"

While the sister's steps fade down the passage, Pell gives the other two his piece in a low voice: show it, don't hand it over, and the stamp stays where it is.

Brother Aldane is grinding something at the worktable, and he finishes the turn of the pestle before he puts it down. He's past sixty, broad, with big clean hands and short white hair. He wears a rose stole over a linen apron stained green-brown at the front. He wipes his hands on a cloth and looks the three of them over, the box last.

Sefa greets him. Then Pell unwraps the vial from its cloth and holds it out, cork in, and asks his questions one after another.

Aldane doesn't take the vial. He doesn't need to. "That's mine. Foxglove, steeped in spirit. I made it up for him at the thaw, when he came in with his heart stumbling on the stairs." He holds up three thick fingers. "Three drops in water, at night. It steadies a weak heart and slows a fast one. Too much and you're sick first. You vomit, you see a yellow ring round every candle, and your heart goes wrong in a way you feel. There was no sick on him, on the floor or in the basin. A finger left in that bottle is about right for a month's use. He didn't take too much, and nobody gave him any."

He answers the rest in the same plain order. "His lips were grey-blue and his nails the same, and his hands were cold to the wrist. That's what a heart that stops does to a man. His eyes were open, and Wenna had closed them by the time I came. There was no smell on him but the drops and old paper. No marks on his throat, his wrists or anywhere else. I looked, because Vell paid for the burial and I wanted to know what I was putting my name to." He nods at the vial. "And who sells it? Nobody. I make it for this infirmary. The herb-wives won't touch foxglove, and they're right not to. I wouldn't trust it from a caravan."

Sefa asks about the room and the wax. He gives her a short look, and there's something gentler in it than in his answers to Pell. "I said the dawn words over him in his chair. The room was a room, mistress. A man died in it, and that doesn't foul a place." Then he lowers himself onto one knee beside the box with a grunt, sets one hand flat on the floor to keep his weight off it, and looks at the seal from a forearm's length without touching it.

He stays there a while.

"That's not funeral wax. I don't know of any." His finger hovers over the scales and doesn't come down. "Those are the Merchantfriend's. Waukeen's, the old way of drawing them. My father kept a bond from her house in the Gate, from before she went quiet in the Troubles. It had green wax like this and scales on it. He wouldn't let us children near it." He looks a moment longer at the closed eye under the beam, and his mouth tightens. "The eye wasn't on his. I've never seen that."

He gets up slowly, one hand on the table edge, and wipes his palms on the cloth again though they're clean.

"He was here the day before he died. Not for his drops. He sat in the second pew from the noon bell until the light went off the east window, and then he came back here and asked me something I've thought about every day since." Aldane folds the cloth in half and lays it on the table. "I'll tell you what he asked. First tell me why three armed people bring a dead clerk's box to a temple instead of to Ostrin Vell, with a man and two bruisers waiting at the bottom of my steps. The sister saw them, and so did I, from the porch."

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets the echo of the pestle settle, then answers without looking away from him. “Because we were hired to carry a box, Brother, and on the road we found a box that had stopped being the one our employer described. Vell told us his red-brown wax would be on it. The wax is green, and it matches a lead stamp the clerk had hidden under his own floorboards.” She says it plainly, as if to a senior sister in the ward. “We didn’t break it. We didn’t sell it to the men at the foot of your steps, though one of them has put eighty gold on the table to carry it away whole and a hundred and twenty if we tell him where we found it and whose seal it carries. That’s Coll Brannock. He asked no questions, named no master, and waited for us on the road like a creditor at a wake.”

She folds her hands at her waist, the prayer beads loose under them. “So before we carry a dead man’s private reckoning under green wax to the man who paid for his funeral, I wanted the one who laid hands on him to look at it. Not to bless the room—you already gave him the dawn words.” A small, careful nod. “To tell us whether the death and the seal ever belonged together.”

She glances at the box, not toward the window. “Vell will pay for delivery. That part is true. But a box that reaches him with the wrong wax and a dead clerk’s hidden stamp inside the story is worth being careful with. If it’s Waukeen’s scales, then it’s a merchant’s keeping, and a shut eye is a bargain signed in the dark. We’d like to know whose bargain.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes the vial back, tucks it into the satchel, and gives the old priest a straight answer.

"Fair question, Brother. Here's the short of it."

He keeps his voice low, for the room and not the novices in the passage.

"Ostrin Vell hired us this morning to fetch that box from Jassan's room, unopened, seal whole. He told us twice what the seal would be: red-brown wax, a V in a ring, his own, put on at his counter the night before Jassan died. We found that instead." He nods at the green. "Nobody's broken it since it was poured, but it isn't Vell's. So either Vell lied to us, or Jassan took his master's seal off and put his own on, and then died the next night. Before we carry it back and get blamed for a seal we didn't break, I wanted to know two things. Did Jassan die on his own? And what are we carrying?" A small tilt of the head. "You've answered the first, and I thank you for it. A tired heart and your drops, honestly taken. That's worth more to me than you'd think."

"The man at the bottom of your steps works for a moneylender up the Trade Way who'd pay well to read Vell's books. He's been following us since the cooper's yard. We're not selling. But a temple porch seemed a better place to think than an alley."

He doesn't mention the stamp in his jerkin.

"So that's why, Brother. Now, what did Jassan ask you?"

He waits for the answer, then adds quietly:

"And that eye under the scales. You said Waukeen's house in the Gate. Is there anyone in the Lower City who still seals in green the old way? A counting-house, a cloth merchant, a priest of hers? The stablehand who ran his letters says they went to the Gate 'care of' somebody, every tenday."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Vell hired us to bring it back unopened. He described red-brown wax with his V. We found this instead, and we’re told breaking it will show the breaker’s face and hand to whoever holds its twin.”

I keep my voice low for the sleeping woman.

“Coll Brannock is outside offering money for it on another lender’s behalf. We haven’t accepted. And Jassan warned a widow that returning this box would bring her husband’s debt due and cost her the house. I wanted advice before we put it in anyone’s hands.”

I glance down at the seal, then back to Aldane.

“We’re not asking you to take sides in a debt. But there’s more here than carrying ledgers across town. What did Jassan ask you?”

scenes.narration:
Brother Aldane hears all three of them out without interrupting. Sefa speaks to him the way a novice reports to a senior sister. Pell keeps his voice low for the passage outside and leaves something out, and the priest's eyes rest on him for a moment as if he's noticed the gap. Bram says it bluntly over the sleeping woman's breathing. When Sefa mentions a stamp hidden under the clerk's floorboards, Aldane glances at the box, then at the three of them, and doesn't ask to see it.

"A widow," he says when Bram finishes. "Which?"

He nods slowly at the name. "Odda Brand. I know her hands. She brings the boy in with his chest every winter." He leaves it there. "A debt is between the people who signed for it. I won't tell you what to do with a box I've not been asked to carry."

He pulls a stool out from under the worktable and sits on it heavily, knees apart and forearms on his apron. He looks older sitting down.

"He asked me this: is a man guilty for what he writes down for others?" He says it the way he'd read a dose off a jar, each word in its place. "I asked him what he meant. He said a clerk writes the sum he's given. He doesn't lend the money, he doesn't sign the note, and he doesn't call it in. He only writes it down true. So is he part of what comes after?"

Aldane looks at his own hands. "I told him a clerk who writes a true sum and doesn't know what it's for has done his work, and no more. But a clerk who comes to know what it's for and keeps on writing has a different question. He should take that one to whoever the sums are hurting, not to a priest." The old woman in the end cot murmurs, and he waits until she's still. "He thought about that a long while. Then he said, 'And if I've written it twice?' I asked him what he meant by twice. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell looks at the three coins a long moment without touching them. Then he looks at the box, and something settles in his face.

"Written it twice," he says quietly, half to himself. "Two books. The one he kept for Vell, and a true copy of what the sums were *for*. Sealed with his own hand so the other hand would know if anyone broke it." He glances at Bram. "Black silver in the alms box. Caravans that never reach Nashkel. A clerk who sits four hours in a pew. I don't like the shape of that, Brother."

To Aldane, plainly:

"Thank you. You've told us more than you had to. Two more things and we'll stop troubling you. Did Jassan say anything else that day, any name, even in passing? Where he was going after, whom he meant to see? And would you keep those coins exactly as they are, out of the poor-box, in case someone wiser than us needs to see them?"

Then he turns to the other two, voice low, for them alone.

"Here's what I think. Vell said nightfall, and it's barely past morning. Coll's sitting at the bottom of the steps waiting for Bram to come down with his arms full. So we don't give him that." He looks back at Aldane. "Brother, would the Song keep a sealed box in its infirmary until this afternoon? Unopened, under your eye, and nobody touches the wax. We'd collect it ourselves, all three of us, before sundown."

If Aldane agrees, Pell goes on to Bram and Sefa:

"Then we walk out light. Feldepost's coach yard first. Dav said Jassan fetched his own replies when the coach was in, and maybe one came after he died that nobody's collected. Then Dobbin at the Juggler, if one of you can stomach him. Harl's train, Zhentarim silver, and a clerk keeping a second book. I'd like to know whether those are one story before we put anything into Vell's hands." A crooked look. "Coll can follow us around town all he likes. A man with empty arms is a dull man to follow."

If Aldane refuses, Pell nods without complaint. "Then we carry it, and we carry it together. Is there a way out through your herb beds that doesn't pass the front steps, Brother? Not to hide. Just so the man at the bottom has to come looking."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’ve seen that tower on the Amn run. Northern outriders carried coins like those—men guarding wagons nobody asked questions about. We called it black silver. It’s a lead, not proof of who paid him.”

I look to Sefa and Pell. “Written twice could mean copies. Or two different sums. We ought to ask Vell before deciding which.”

Then I turn back to Aldane. “Would you come to his counter with us? Not to judge the debt. To witness that we found green wax and returned it untouched, and hear his explanation. I’d also ask him what payment would release Odda’s house in full. Between us, we may have an honest way to help her.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stands very still while Aldane rolls the old silver back into its cloth, and some quiet thing behind her eyes finishes working itself out.

“Zhentil Keep silver in Jassan’s hand,” she says at last, more to herself than the room. “Black silver, to road men. And the day before he died he gave it away, all three pieces, to the poor-box.” She looks from the cloth to the green seal on the floor. “A man who thought himself guilty wouldn’t spend them. He’d shed them, like a fever. I’ve seen men do the same with coins they earned in a trade they’d begun to call sin.”

She paces once, a short turn between the worktable and the window, then stops.

“He wrote it twice. Not once for Vell’s books — twice.” Her voice drops, but carries in the whitewashed quiet. “He was keeping a second record beyond his master’s reach, or copying the true sums into a second hand’s keeping. The letters to the Lower City, ‘care of’ some name he wouldn’t put on the outside — that was the other half of the bargain. And the seal and stamp are a clerk’s way of forcing a witness.” She points two fingers toward the box without approaching it. “One hand of two. The other sees. If Vell breaks that wax, the other hand sees Vell’s face at the moment he opens it. If we break it, the other hand sees ours. That’s why Jassan hid the stamp and left the box behind. He wanted it to be opened — but by the right hand, at the right time, before the other debtor ran out of patience.”

She turns to Pell and Bram. “I don’t think the seal marks whose bargain. It marks that the bargain was twofold, and that one party was not meant to walk away unseen.”

Then, to Aldane: “You gave him a good answer, Brother. Better than he could carry.” Her voice is gentler now. “He sat in your pew four hours and then went home to his own heart. If the heart stopped, it stopped under a weight, and the weight was a double set of sums.”

She looks at the old woman by the wall, the long clean cots, the violet window-light. “Will you do two things for us? Keep those three coins separate and your word about his body close, in case the Fist or Vell asks. And tell us if there’s a road off this hill that doesn’t pass your front steps — a garden gate, a way through to the wood beyond the wall. The men outside can wait for dust, but I’d rather we choose our own hour.”
