scenes.narration:
Pell looks at the three coins a long while without touching them. Then he looks at the box. He says it half to himself first: two books, the one Jassan kept for Vell and a true copy of what the sums were for. Then he says the rest aloud to the priest. Black silver in the alms box, caravans that never reach Nashkel, a clerk who sat four hours in a pew. He doesn't like the shape of it. He thanks Aldane and asks his last two things: did Jassan name anyone that day, or say where he was going, and will Aldane keep the coins just as they are? Then, low, to Bram and Sefa, he lays out his plan. The box stays here, they walk out with empty hands, and they go to Feldepost's and then to Dobbin. Then he turns back to Aldane and asks whether the Song will hold a sealed box in its infirmary until the afternoon.

Bram tells Aldane where he has seen the tower before: the Amn run, the northern outriders, the coin caravan men called black silver. He says it's a lead and not proof. *Written twice* could mean copies or two different sums, and he wants to put it to Vell before anyone decides which. Then he asks the priest to come to Vell's counter as a witness. He wouldn't be there to judge the debt, only to say the wax was green and came back untouched. While they're there, Bram means to ask Vell what sum would clear Odda's house outright.

Sefa stands still while the cloth is rolled over the silver. When she speaks, it's the end of something she has been working through. A man who thought himself guilty wouldn't spend those coins, he'd get rid of them, and she has watched men do the same with wages from a trade they'd come to call a sin. She walks once between the table and the window and gives her reading of the seal and the twin hand. Then she speaks to the priest more gently: he gave Jassan a good answer, better than Jassan could carry. She asks two things of him: keep the coins apart and keep his word about the body close. And is there a way off the hill that doesn't run past his front steps?

Aldane hears them out on his stool and answers in the order he was asked, the way he'd go down a row of cots.

"No name. He didn't say where he was going." He thinks about it honestly. "He asked me one thing on his way to the door that I took for nothing. Whether the Fist ever comes to the dawn rite. I told him one sergeant does, Cowl, most mornings. Sits at the back and leaves before the hymn." He gets up, opens the small drawer under the jars, puts the twist of cloth inside and shuts it. "The coins stay as they are. Nobody spends them."

He looks at the box by Bram's boot, then at Pell. "Keep it here? No, Master Dunmore. Not on its own. If Vell comes asking who has his ledgers, or that man at my steps does, I want to be able to say *the people who brought them*. I won't be its keeper." He nods at the empty cot beside the worktable. "It can sit here as long as one of you sits with it. I'll not have it stolen out of a sick-room, and nobody will lay a hand on it while I'm in this room. That's as far as I'll go."

To Bram: "I won't come to Vell's counter. I have her." He tips his head at the end cot. "But I'll write down what I saw." He pulls a scrap of good paper toward him and dips a pen. The hand that comes out is broad and slow, a hand that labels jars. *Seen at the Song of the Morning this day, toward the fourth hour after dawn: an oak strongbox, iron at the corners, sealed over the lock in dark green wax upon lead, the mark a pair of scales above a closed eye. The seal whole and unbroken. Brought by Bram Halloway and two others who carry it for Ostrin Vell. Aldane, of the Morninglord's house.* He warms a stub of rose-coloured wax at the lamp, presses a small brass sun into it and lays the paper on the table beside the mortar. "What Vell asks for Mistress Brand's roof is between you and Vell. I'd like to know the answer. That's all."

He turns to Sefa last, and his voice is no softer than it was for the others. "I'll keep the coins apart. My word about his body I won't keep close. If the Fist asks, or Vell, or you again, I'll tell them his own heart stopped. I don't tell it differently for anyone." He points through the window, south over the herb beds. "The way off the hill is the little gate at the bottom of the sage. It goes into the burial ground. He's in there, the new mound by the yew. Past the graves a lane runs round the hill and comes out on the Trade Way by the first houses north of here. It isn't hidden. You can see where it comes out from the road if you look."

They look. Past the sage and rosemary, a hurdle gate stands in a low wall, and beyond it the burial ground slopes away under a single dark yew, with a fresh brown mound at its foot. At the far side, where the lane runs off round the hill, a man thick through the shoulders sits on the boundary wall in a carter's smock that doesn't fit him. His boots dangle over the lane. He is working his way through one of the almshouse rolls.

In the end cot the old woman wakes, blinks at the whitewash and turns her head until she finds the man in mail. "If you've come to carry me out, you can wait," she tells Bram, clear as a bell. "I've not had my bread." Aldane is already filling a cup at the ewer. On the worktable lie the priest's note, still warm under its rose-coloured wax, and the shut drawer with the black silver in it. By Bram's boot the green eye on the box faces the ceiling.

 (Out of game) None of the four needed a roll: they were plain requests put to Aldane, and he answered each one in the scene from his own reasons. He gave no name, he agreed to keep the coins, he won't keep the box unless one of you sits with it, and he won't go to Vell's but wrote a witness note instead. If Pell or Bram wants to press him, say how and I'll call a Persuasion check.

relay.request:
Characters at the table: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.
In this scene: Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin.
Write the screens of, in this order: Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Pell Dunmore: Pell looks at the three coins a long moment without touching them. Then he looks at the box, and something settles in his face.

"Written it twice," he says quietly, half to himself. "Two books. The one he kept for Vell, and a true copy of what the sums were *for*. Sealed with his own hand so the other hand would know if anyone broke it." He glances at Bram. "Black silver in the alms box. Caravans that never reach Nashkel. A clerk who sits four hours in a pew. I don't like the shape of that, Brother."

To Aldane, plainly:

"Thank you. You've told us more than you had to. Two more things and we'll stop troubling you. Did Jassan say anything else that day, any name, even in passing? Where he was going after, whom he meant to see? And would you keep those coins exactly as they are, out of the poor-box, in case someone wiser than us needs to see them?"

Then he turns to the other two, voice low, for them alone.

"Here's what I think. Vell said nightfall, and it's barely past morning. Coll's sitting at the bottom of the steps waiting for Bram to come down with his arms full. So we don't give him that." He looks back at Aldane. "Brother, would the Song keep a sealed box in its infirmary until this afternoon? Unopened, under your eye, and nobody touches the wax. We'd collect it ourselves, all three of us, before sundown."

If Aldane agrees, Pell goes on to Bram and Sefa:

"Then we walk out light. Feldepost's coach yard first. Dav said Jassan fetched his own replies when the coach was in, and maybe one came after he died that nobody's collected. Then Dobbin at the Juggler, if one of you can stomach him. Harl's train, Zhentarim silver, and a clerk keeping a second book. I'd like to know whether those are one story before we put anything into Vell's hands." A crooked look. "Coll can follow us around town all he likes. A man with empty arms is a dull man to follow."

If Aldane refuses, Pell nods without complaint. "Then we carry it, and we carry it together. Is there a way out through your herb beds that doesn't pass the front steps, Brother? Not to hide. Just so the man at the bottom has to come looking."

Bram Halloway: “I’ve seen that tower on the Amn run. Northern outriders carried coins like those—men guarding wagons nobody asked questions about. We called it black silver. It’s a lead, not proof of who paid him.”

I look to Sefa and Pell. “Written twice could mean copies. Or two different sums. We ought to ask Vell before deciding which.”

Then I turn back to Aldane. “Would you come to his counter with us? Not to judge the debt. To witness that we found green wax and returned it untouched, and hear his explanation. I’d also ask him what payment would release Odda’s house in full. Between us, we may have an honest way to help her.”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa stands very still while Aldane rolls the old silver back into its cloth, and some quiet thing behind her eyes finishes working itself out.

“Zhentil Keep silver in Jassan’s hand,” she says at last, more to herself than the room. “Black silver, to road men. And the day before he died he gave it away, all three pieces, to the poor-box.” She looks from the cloth to the green seal on the floor. “A man who thought himself guilty wouldn’t spend them. He’d shed them, like a fever. I’ve seen men do the same with coins they earned in a trade they’d begun to call sin.”

She paces once, a short turn between the worktable and the window, then stops.

“He wrote it twice. Not once for Vell’s books — twice.” Her voice drops, but carries in the whitewashed quiet. “He was keeping a second record beyond his master’s reach, or copying the true sums into a second hand’s keeping. The letters to the Lower City, ‘care of’ some name he wouldn’t put on the outside — that was the other half of the bargain. And the seal and stamp are a clerk’s way of forcing a witness.” She points two fingers toward the box without approaching it. “One hand of two. The other sees. If Vell breaks that wax, the other hand sees Vell’s face at the moment he opens it. If we break it, the other hand sees ours. That’s why Jassan hid the stamp and left the box behind. He wanted it to be opened — but by the right hand, at the right time, before the other debtor ran out of patience.”

She turns to Pell and Bram. “I don’t think the seal marks whose bargain. It marks that the bargain was twofold, and that one party was not meant to walk away unseen.”

Then, to Aldane: “You gave him a good answer, Brother. Better than he could carry.” Her voice is gentler now. “He sat in your pew four hours and then went home to his own heart. If the heart stopped, it stopped under a weight, and the weight was a double set of sums.”

She looks at the old woman by the wall, the long clean cots, the violet window-light. “Will you do two things for us? Keep those three coins separate and your word about his body close, in case the Fist or Vell asks. And tell us if there’s a road off this hill that doesn’t pass your front steps — a garden gate, a way through to the wood beyond the wall. The men outside can wait for dust, but I’d rather we choose our own hour.”

Your narration:
<<<
Pell looks at the three coins a long while without touching them. Then he looks at the box. He says it half to himself first: two books, the one Jassan kept for Vell and a true copy of what the sums were for. Then he says the rest aloud to the priest. Black silver in the alms box, caravans that never reach Nashkel, a clerk who sat four hours in a pew. He doesn't like the shape of it. He thanks Aldane and asks his last two things: did Jassan name anyone that day, or say where he was going, and will Aldane keep the coins just as they are? Then, low, to Bram and Sefa, he lays out his plan. The box stays here, they walk out with empty hands, and they go to Feldepost's and then to Dobbin. Then he turns back to Aldane and asks whether the Song will hold a sealed box in its infirmary until the afternoon.

Bram tells Aldane where he has seen the tower before: the Amn run, the northern outriders, the coin caravan men called black silver. He says it's a lead and not proof. *Written twice* could mean copies or two different sums, and he wants to put it to Vell before anyone decides which. Then he asks the priest to come to Vell's counter as a witness. He wouldn't be there to judge the debt, only to say the wax was green and came back untouched. While they're there, Bram means to ask Vell what sum would clear Odda's house outright.

Sefa stands still while the cloth is rolled over the silver. When she speaks, it's the end of something she has been working through. A man who thought himself guilty wouldn't spend those coins, he'd get rid of them, and she has watched men do the same with wages from a trade they'd come to call a sin. She walks once between the table and the window and gives her reading of the seal and the twin hand. Then she speaks to the priest more gently: he gave Jassan a good answer, better than Jassan could carry. She asks two things of him: keep the coins apart and keep his word about the body close. And is there a way off the hill that doesn't run past his front steps?

Aldane hears them out on his stool and answers in the order he was asked, the way he'd go down a row of cots.

"No name. He didn't say where he was going." He thinks about it honestly. "He asked me one thing on his way to the door that I took for nothing. Whether the Fist ever comes to the dawn rite. I told him one sergeant does, Cowl, most mornings. Sits at the back and leaves before the hymn." He gets up, opens the small drawer under the jars, puts the twist of cloth inside and shuts it. "The coins stay as they are. Nobody spends them."

He looks at the box by Bram's boot, then at Pell. "Keep it here? No, Master Dunmore. Not on its own. If Vell comes asking who has his ledgers, or that man at my steps does, I want to be able to say *the people who brought them*. I won't be its keeper." He nods at the empty cot beside the worktable. "It can sit here as long as one of you sits with it. I'll not have it stolen out of a sick-room, and nobody will lay a hand on it while I'm in this room. That's as far as I'll go."

To Bram: "I won't come to Vell's counter. I have her." He tips his head at the end cot. "But I'll write down what I saw." He pulls a scrap of good paper toward him and dips a pen. The hand that comes out is broad and slow, a hand that labels jars. *Seen at the Song of the Morning this day, toward the fourth hour after dawn: an oak strongbox, iron at the corners, sealed over the lock in dark green wax upon lead, the mark a pair of scales above a closed eye. The seal whole and unbroken. Brought by Bram Halloway and two others who carry it for Ostrin Vell. Aldane, of the Morninglord's house.* He warms a stub of rose-coloured wax at the lamp, presses a small brass sun into it and lays the paper on the table beside the mortar. "What Vell asks for Mistress Brand's roof is between you and Vell. I'd like to know the answer. That's all."

He turns to Sefa last, and his voice is no softer than it was for the others. "I'll keep the coins apart. My word about his body I won't keep close. If the Fist asks, or Vell, or you again, I'll tell them his own heart stopped. I don't tell it differently for anyone." He points through the window, south over the herb beds. "The way off the hill is the little gate at the bottom of the sage. It goes into the burial ground. He's in there, the new mound by the yew. Past the graves a lane runs round the hill and comes out on the Trade Way by the first houses north of here. It isn't hidden. You can see where it comes out from the road if you look."

They look. Past the sage and rosemary, a hurdle gate stands in a low wall, and beyond it the burial ground slopes away under a single dark yew, with a fresh brown mound at its foot. At the far side, where the lane runs off round the hill, a man thick through the shoulders sits on the boundary wall in a carter's smock that doesn't fit him. His boots dangle over the lane. He is working his way through one of the almshouse rolls.

In the end cot the old woman wakes, blinks at the whitewash and turns her head until she finds the man in mail. "If you've come to carry me out, you can wait," she tells Bram, clear as a bell. "I've not had my bread." Aldane is already filling a cup at the ewer. On the worktable lie the priest's note, still warm under its rose-coloured wax, and the shut drawer with the black silver in it. By Bram's boot the green eye on the box faces the ceiling.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“No carrying anyone out, mistress. I’m waiting too.”

I take Aldane’s written statement with a nod of thanks, then pull a stool beside the box.

“I’ll stay with it. Pell, Sefa—follow up the coach yard and Dobbin if you think that’s our best lead. Ask where Sergeant Cowl can be found, too. Ferr may have meant to speak to him.”

I keep my voice low. “The smock man’s watching the burial-ground lane. Don’t mistake that way for clear. And come back well before dusk—we still owe Vell an answer today.”

I settle my shield within reach, with the box beside my boots.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa moves a step nearer to the window and stands where she can see the burial ground and the lane without putting her whole face into the light. Her arms fold lightly across her middle.

“He’s put a man on the back way too. A carter’s smock that doesn’t fit, eating a temple roll and watching the lane.” She says it without alarm, the same way she once noted a fever had turned in the night. “So they’ve thought about the hill, not just the steps. If we all go down by the graves, he’ll know we’ve no box with us, and so will the other three before we’re past the first houses. Better to leave as we came, empty-handed, walking like people with a warm breadcrumb to share.”

She turns back to the room, but keeps one eye on the window.

“Here’s what I advise. The box stays in this room with Bram. Brother Aldane said he won’t be its keeper, but as long as one of us sits with it, no one lays a hand on it. Bram’s better suited than either of us to sit by it, and Coll won’t try the temple with two of us still at large. Pell and I go to Feldepost’s coach yard and ask for the name Jassan Ferr’s letters were sent and received against. That’s a thread we can follow in daylight. If it runs to the Fist, so be it; if it runs to Thale’s people, so much the better.”

She looks to Pell. “I can put a good face on a coachman and read whatever board he’s pinned his bags to. And if the pair of us are followed from the steps, we’ll see it and split in the alley beside the Juggler. We’re no one’s escort if we’re not carrying the box.”

Then she glances down at the priest’s rose-waxed note still on the table, and at Aldane.

“Brother, a last thing. When Jassan asked whether the Fist came to the dawn rite, did he ask it like a man seeking a sergeant for his own sake, or like a man easing his mind about when he’d be able to find one?” She softens it with a half-smile. “If the latter, he may have carried his double set of sums as far as the Fist post the morning before he died.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes Aldane's sealed note from beside the mortar, checks the rose wax without breaking it, and tucks it inside his jerkin with Vell's.

"Thank you, Brother. That's more than fair." He gives the old woman a small bow. "Nobody's carrying you anywhere, mother. He only carries boxes."

Then, low, to Bram and Sefa:

"Here's how I'd split it. Bram stays with the box. He's got the arms for it, the mail, and a priest in the room. Nobody's dragging it past him in a temple. Sefa, stay or come, your choice. If you come, you're better with a coachman than I am, and I'd like a second pair of eyes on whoever follows." A glance at the herb beds and the man on the wall. "I'm not going out the back. He's sat there to watch for a box going that way. Let him watch an empty gate."

"I go out the front, hands empty, right past Coll. He'll see I'm not carrying and have to choose. Split his three, or keep them all on this hill. Either way he learns less than he'd like. I'll go to Feldepost's coach yard and ask after any post for Jassan Ferr that came after he died, and what name the coachman laughed at. If there's time, I'll pass the Fist post and see if Sergeant Cowl's about. Jassan asked whether the Fist comes to the dawn rite. Nobody asks that unless they mean to talk to one." He touches the place where the stamp sits. "The stamp stays on me. Box here, stamp there. Nobody gets both by grabbing one of us."

"I'll be back well before the light turns. If I'm not back by the afternoon bell, don't come looking. Carry it to Vell with Aldane's note and both of you."

He waits for their nods. Then he goes back through the nave and out onto the porch, and walks down the hollowed steps at an easy pace, thumbs in his belt so his empty hands show.

At the bottom he gives Coll the same short nod as before, and in roof cadence, light: *"House is shut, the goods stay in."* Meaning: *it's not on me, and it's not coming out yet.*

He doesn't wait for an answer. He turns north up the Trade Way toward town and Feldepost's. Where a cart or a doorway gives him a reflection or an angle, he checks who has peeled off to follow him: Coll himself, the jerkin man, or nobody.

scenes.narration:
Bram takes the folded note from beside the mortar with a nod of thanks. The rose wax is still a little soft under his thumb. He tucks it away, pulls a stool out from under the end of the worktable and sets it next to the box. "No carrying anyone out, mistress. I'm waiting too."

The old woman looks him up and down, at the mail, the shield and the oak box at his boots, and seems to decide he'll do as furniture. "Then wait quieter. You creak."

A moment after Bram, Pell reaches for the same note and his fingers come down on bare wood beside the mortar. It's already gone into Bram's belt. He turns the movement into a small bow to the end cot. "Nobody's carrying you anywhere, mother. He only carries boxes." The old woman doesn't answer. Aldane has put a cup of water in her hands and a roll from the almshouse basket in her lap, and she has better things to do.

Bram keeps his voice low and gives his piece. He'll stay with the box. Pell and Sefa can follow up the coach yard and Dobbin if they think that's the best lead, and ask where Sergeant Cowl can be found. The smock man is on the burial-ground lane, so that way isn't clear. And they should be back well before dusk. He sets the shield against his knee, within reach, and puts one boot against the oak.

Sefa has moved to the window and stands to one side of it, so the light falls on her shoulder and not her face. Past the sage and the hurdle gate the man in the smock is still on the boundary wall, his boots hanging over the lane, picking crumbs off his front. She tells the other two what she sees and what she'd do. The box stays with Bram. She and Pell leave the way they came, with empty hands, and go to Feldepost's for the name on Jassan's letters. If anyone follows them, they split in the alley by the Juggler. Then she turns to Aldane with her question about Cowl and a half-smile to soften it.

Aldane has gone back to his stool. He thinks about it before he answers.

"For his own sake? I can't tell you what was in him, mistress. I can tell you how he asked it. He had his hat on and his hand on the door. He asked if the Fist came to the dawn rite, and I told him about Cowl. Then he asked which bell the rite begins at. I said the first." He holds up one thick finger, as if it were a dose. "He said, 'Tomorrow, then.' Not to me. The way a man tells himself where he's put his boots." He lowers the hand. "He was dead before the first bell. Wenna Pike's man came for me at second."

Pell has already gone. While Sefa was still putting her question, he said the rest of his plan low at Bram's shoulder. Bram stays with the box, Sefa comes or stays as she likes, and the stamp stays on Pell: box here, stamp there. If he isn't back by the afternoon bell, they carry the box to Vell with the priest's note and don't come looking for him. Then he went down the side passage, past the two novices, who went back to their bandages in a hurry, and out through the nave.

The porch is bright after the whitewash. The freckled sister is sweeping the last step. The old almsman has eaten one roll and is starting on the second. Pell comes down the hollowed steps at an easy pace with his thumbs in his belt, so anyone can see his hands are empty.

Coll Brannock is still on the packed dust at the bottom, off the stone, as he promised. The jerkin man stands on the near verge. Coll watches Pell come down and doesn't move until Pell is level with him.

Pell gives him the short nod. *"House is shut, the goods stay in."*

Coll's eyes go over him once, belt, jerkin, hands, the way a man counts a purse he isn't allowed to open. He answers in the same rise and fall: *"Then the doorman eats well."* On the roofs that means *I'll keep the door.* Then, still in cant and quieter, as if remembering the weather: *"Heard that line on the Wide once. From a boy no taller than the chimney pots."* He smiles a little, says nothing else, and looks back up at the rose-coloured doors. He doesn't use any name. He lifts two fingers from his belt and lowers them.

Pell walks north. The Trade Way is as busy as before: a charcoal wagon going the other way, a woman driving geese, two Amnian drovers arguing over a halter. Thirty paces on, the brass basin hanging outside a barber's door gives him the road behind him at a slant. Coll is still at the foot of the steps. The jerkin man has left the verge and is walking north at an idle sort of pace, about sixty feet back, on the far side of the road. He isn't trying to hide. The smock man isn't on the road at all.

Past the horse trough the town closes in, with hammers again and smithy smoke. Feldepost's is easy to find: a long, two-storey front of timber over stone on the Trade Way, a painted sign of a post-horn, and a wide arch beside it into the coach yard. Through the arch there are cobbles, a long stable, and a water butt. Under the arch hangs a slate chalked in a round hand: *GATE COACH — IN at the afternoon bell. OUT at first light.*

The post is kept in a plank booth built into the arch, with a half-door and a rack of pigeonholes behind it. The woman in it is stout and grey-haired, with spectacles on a cord. She's sorting a sack of letters into the rack without looking at the outsides more than she has to. She hears Pell's questions out with a letter still in her hand.

"Jassan Ferr. Vell's clerk." She puts the letter in its hole. "I heard. Shame. He was always civil, and he always had his coppers ready." She turns to the rack, reaches to the top row and taps one pigeonhole without taking out what's in it. It's a thick packet, folded and tied, and a dark green blob of wax shows at the edge. "That came in on the last coach, two days back. For him, to wait here. He's never kept anything waiting before. He'd be in the yard before the horses were out of the traces." She takes her hand away. "It's his, and it stays his. If somebody stands for him with something to show for it, they can talk to me. Otherwise it goes back north on the coach at the tenday's end, the same as any post nobody collects."

As for the name, she snorts. "That's no secret. Hobb, the coachman, bawled it across the yard every time he bagged one of Ferr's, because he thought it was a fine lady's way to address a letter. *Gate, Lower City, care of Ilmara Venn, scrivener, Bloomridge.*" She says it in Hobb's voice, with a flourish on *care of*. "Hobb's on the coach. You can ask him yourself at the afternoon bell if you want it with the laugh."

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Bram Halloway: “No carrying anyone out, mistress. I’m waiting too.”

I take Aldane’s written statement with a nod of thanks, then pull a stool beside the box.

“I’ll stay with it. Pell, Sefa—follow up the coach yard and Dobbin if you think that’s our best lead. Ask where Sergeant Cowl can be found, too. Ferr may have meant to speak to him.”

I keep my voice low. “The smock man’s watching the burial-ground lane. Don’t mistake that way for clear. And come back well before dusk—we still owe Vell an answer today.”

I settle my shield within reach, with the box beside my boots.

Sefa Marrin: Sefa moves a step nearer to the window and stands where she can see the burial ground and the lane without putting her whole face into the light. Her arms fold lightly across her middle.

“He’s put a man on the back way too. A carter’s smock that doesn’t fit, eating a temple roll and watching the lane.” She says it without alarm, the same way she once noted a fever had turned in the night. “So they’ve thought about the hill, not just the steps. If we all go down by the graves, he’ll know we’ve no box with us, and so will the other three before we’re past the first houses. Better to leave as we came, empty-handed, walking like people with a warm breadcrumb to share.”

She turns back to the room, but keeps one eye on the window.

“Here’s what I advise. The box stays in this room with Bram. Brother Aldane said he won’t be its keeper, but as long as one of us sits with it, no one lays a hand on it. Bram’s better suited than either of us to sit by it, and Coll won’t try the temple with two of us still at large. Pell and I go to Feldepost’s coach yard and ask for the name Jassan Ferr’s letters were sent and received against. That’s a thread we can follow in daylight. If it runs to the Fist, so be it; if it runs to Thale’s people, so much the better.”

She looks to Pell. “I can put a good face on a coachman and read whatever board he’s pinned his bags to. And if the pair of us are followed from the steps, we’ll see it and split in the alley beside the Juggler. We’re no one’s escort if we’re not carrying the box.”

Then she glances down at the priest’s rose-waxed note still on the table, and at Aldane.

“Brother, a last thing. When Jassan asked whether the Fist came to the dawn rite, did he ask it like a man seeking a sergeant for his own sake, or like a man easing his mind about when he’d be able to find one?” She softens it with a half-smile. “If the latter, he may have carried his double set of sums as far as the Fist post the morning before he died.”

Pell Dunmore: Pell takes Aldane's sealed note from beside the mortar, checks the rose wax without breaking it, and tucks it inside his jerkin with Vell's.

"Thank you, Brother. That's more than fair." He gives the old woman a small bow. "Nobody's carrying you anywhere, mother. He only carries boxes."

Then, low, to Bram and Sefa:

"Here's how I'd split it. Bram stays with the box. He's got the arms for it, the mail, and a priest in the room. Nobody's dragging it past him in a temple. Sefa, stay or come, your choice. If you come, you're better with a coachman than I am, and I'd like a second pair of eyes on whoever follows." A glance at the herb beds and the man on the wall. "I'm not going out the back. He's sat there to watch for a box going that way. Let him watch an empty gate."

"I go out the front, hands empty, right past Coll. He'll see I'm not carrying and have to choose. Split his three, or keep them all on this hill. Either way he learns less than he'd like. I'll go to Feldepost's coach yard and ask after any post for Jassan Ferr that came after he died, and what name the coachman laughed at. If there's time, I'll pass the Fist post and see if Sergeant Cowl's about. Jassan asked whether the Fist comes to the dawn rite. Nobody asks that unless they mean to talk to one." He touches the place where the stamp sits. "The stamp stays on me. Box here, stamp there. Nobody gets both by grabbing one of us."

"I'll be back well before the light turns. If I'm not back by the afternoon bell, don't come looking. Carry it to Vell with Aldane's note and both of you."

He waits for their nods. Then he goes back through the nave and out onto the porch, and walks down the hollowed steps at an easy pace, thumbs in his belt so his empty hands show.

At the bottom he gives Coll the same short nod as before, and in roof cadence, light: *"House is shut, the goods stay in."* Meaning: *it's not on me, and it's not coming out yet.*

He doesn't wait for an answer. He turns north up the Trade Way toward town and Feldepost's. Where a cart or a doorway gives him a reflection or an angle, he checks who has peeled off to follow him: Coll himself, the jerkin man, or nobody.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.

opening.narration:
Beregost wakes to hammers. From every smithy along the street the ringing comes through the shutters of Ostrin Vell's counting-house, where the morning light falls on brass scales and rows of bound ledgers. Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway stand at the long counter. The three of you met here only this morning, and Vell has just hired you together.

Vell lays the terms out a second time, tapping the counter with one finger at each point. Jassan Ferr, his clerk, died three days ago in a rented room above the cooper's yard on the Coast Way. In that room is a locked strongbox of ledgers. Vell wants it here before nightfall today, unopened, with its seal whole. On delivery he will pay seventy-five gold for the three of you to share. Not a copper before.

Beside the counter stands a clerk's desk. Its stool is pushed neatly under it, the inkwell is capped and the blotter is clean, as if someone had tidied it and no one had sat there since. Vell does not look at it. He looks from Sefa to Pell to Bram, folds his hands on the counter and waits. "The Coast Way is not far, and the day will not wait for you. Is there anything you need to ask me before you go?"

- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.

screens.text:
The session begins.

Beregost wakes to hammers. From every smithy along the street the ringing comes through the shutters of Ostrin Vell's counting-house, where the morning light falls on brass scales and rows of bound ledgers. You stand at the long counter with Sefa Marrin and Pell Dunmore, whom you met only this morning, and Vell has just hired the three of you together.

Vell lays out the terms a second time, tapping the counter with one finger at each point. Jassan Ferr, his clerk, died three days ago in a rented room above the cooper's yard on the Coast Way. In that room is a locked strongbox of ledgers. Vell wants it here before nightfall today, unopened, with its seal whole. On delivery he will pay seventy-five gold for the three of you to share. Not a copper before.

Beside the counter stands a clerk's desk. Its stool is pushed neatly under it, the inkwell is capped and the blotter is clean, as if someone had tidied it and no one had sat there since. Vell does not look at it. He looks from Sefa to Pell to you, folds his hands on the counter and waits. "The Coast Way is not far, and the day will not wait for you. Is there anything you need to ask me before you go?"

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10
Skills: Athletics +6; Perception +4; Survival +4; Intimidation +3; Tools: land vehicles +3
Saves: Strength saving throw +6 (proficient); Constitution saving throw +5 (proficient); Dexterity saving throw +1; Intelligence saving throw +0; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +0
Attacks: Longsword +6 to hit, 1d8+3 slashing (1d10+3 two-handed); Javelin +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 30/120; Extra Attack: two attacks with the Attack action
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Extra Attack: attacks twice when taking the Attack action; Fighting style, Protection: with a shield, a reaction imposes disadvantage on an attack against a creature within 5 feet of him; Second Wind: a bonus action, regains 1d10+5 hit points; once per short rest; Action Surge: one additional action on his turn; once per short rest; Improved Critical (Champion): a weapon attack crits on 19 or 20; Healer's kit: stabilises a dying creature without a check (ten uses)
Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Second wind 1/1; Action surge 1/1; Heroic inspiration 0/1

Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: Ostrin Vell's counting-house, at the long counter · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa glances at the empty, spotless clerk's desk, then back at Vell, and keeps her hands still rather than fidgeting with her prayer beads. In a quiet, clear voice she asks whether Jassan died of fever. She asks who has gone into the room since his death, and whether a key exists or whether you must ask the cooper to open the dead man's door.

Pell props an elbow on the counter, at ease, his gaze resting on the empty desk for a moment before it returns to Vell. He counts questions off on his fingers. He asks how Jassan died, and whether a knife was involved. He asks what the box looks like, who holds the key, and who else knows it is there. He asks whether anyone has been in the room since, and whether the landlord expects you. He also asks whether Vell still wants the box found if someone has already taken it. He watches Vell's face and hands as he asks.

Vell does not look at the desk. He keeps his eyes on whoever is speaking and waits until all three of you have finished. He answers in the order he likes.

"His heart." He says it to Sefa first. "Not fever. Wenna Pike, the landlady, found him in the morning, in his chair. The Song of the Morning sent a priest to look at him. There was no mark on him. They buried him yesterday. I paid for it." He gives Pell a short glance. "No knife, Master Dunmore. If there had been one, the Fist would be in that room and you would not."

He spreads his fingers on the counter, as if measuring. "Oak, iron at the corners, about the length of my forearm. Two handles. It's heavy. One of you will want to carry it with both arms." He touches his waistcoat over the breastbone, where something small and hard sits under the cloth. "I have the key. Not him. Nobody opens it on the way, so nobody needs a key." Then he answers the seal question a little faster than the others, the way a man says a thing he has already said to himself: "My seal is over the lock. Red-brown wax, a V in a ring. You will see it."

"Who else knows the box is there?" He thinks about it honestly. "Wenna Pike. She has the key to his room, so you ask her. The cooper downstairs, Tobin, perhaps. Jassan had no family here. His mother was a clerk in the Gate, and she has been dead for years." He pauses. "Anyone he owed, I don't know. He didn't tell me his debts. If Wenna wants his rent, that is Jassan's debt. Not mine."

To you he gives the longest look. "Dispute it? The ledgers are mine. The box is mine." He breathes out through his nose. "There is a man on the Trade Way named Gerrit Thale. He lends money, as I do, and he would like very much to read my books. He has not been told about this box. That does not mean he hasn't heard. That is part of the seventy-five. The rest is haste, and keeping quiet. My clients' sums are my clients' business."

He turns to Pell. "If someone has carried it off, find it. Same terms. Same nightfall."

He takes a sheet from under the counter, uncaps his inkwell and writes four lines in a small, upright hand without hesitating. He folds it twice, warms a stick of red-brown wax over the lamp and presses a ring from his left hand into it, a V inside a circle. He slides the note to the middle of the counter. It says that the bearers act for Ostrin Vell and are to receive Jassan Ferr's strongbox.

"Show that to Wenna Pike. Follow the Coast Way past the third smithy; the cooper's yard has barrels stacked at the gate." He pulls the brass scales toward him and sets a weight in the pan, already a moneylender at his morning work. Outside the shutters the hammers keep ringing. The light has moved a hand's width along the ledgers on the shelf. The clerk's stool stays pushed in under the empty desk.

On the questions he skipped, Vell sets the weight down. "Wenna. The priest who looked at him. The two men who carried him down to the temple. I have not been up there." He says the last part flatly. "Does she know you're coming? No. I sent no word. Show her the note."

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Vell's strongbox
+ Quest: Vell's strongbox

Where you are: Ostrin Vell's counting-room · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Pell's hand gets to the note first. He runs a thumbnail along the edge of the wax without lifting it and slips the sheet inside his jerkin. You and Sefa reach for it a moment later and find bare wood.

Pell asks Vell, casually, when he put his seal on the box, before it went home with the dead man or after, so he knows whether the wax should be fresh or old.

Vell answers in the same breath. "Before. Here, on this counter, the evening before he died. My ring, my wax. I locked it and he carried it home." His hand moves to his waistcoat, over the breastbone, then away. "I wanted it out of this house for a few days. That is my reason, and it stays mine. The wax will be four days old."

He turns to you. "As it stands, then. If it's broken, bring it broken. Then I'll know." To Sefa he gives a short, dry look, and the corner of his mouth doesn't move. "The town checks my scales every spring, Mistress Marrin. They have never been found light." He is already looking down at the weights when the door closes behind the three of you.

Sefa says she wants to see the room before half of Beregost hears that three hirelings are asking after a dead man's ledgers. Pell nods at the tidy desk and says you'll be back before nightfall. Once you are out in the street among the hammers, he comes alongside you and Sefa and says in a low voice that Vell answered the seal question before he'd finished asking it, and that Vell has never set foot in that room. If someone has opened the box and resealed it, Vell will say it was you. So nobody touches the box until all three of you have looked at the wax together. He keeps his eyes on the street as you walk.

The Coast Way is full of noise and smoke. A cart of pig iron grinds past, and its driver shouts at a dog. Two apprentices carry a quench-tub between them with water slopping over the rim. A woman beats a rug from an upstairs window. Pell looks down the street and back, at doorways, corners and the bench outside the chandler's. A carter is watering his mule. An old man sleeps against a wall in the sun. No one is waiting outside Vell's door, and no one starts walking when you do.

You count the smithies. The third is a farrier's, open to the street, where a horse stands with one hoof up and a boy holds its head. Past it the noise thins. The cooper's yard is where Vell said: a plank gate standing half open, with new barrels stacked three high on either side and the smell of shavings and wet oak coming out of it. Inside, someone hammers hoops in a slow, steady rhythm. A wooden stair climbs the outside wall of the house to a door on the upper floor.

The left gatepost has been chalked low down, about knee height, where a passer-by's eye wouldn't go: a small circle with a short stroke through it and a dot above. The chalk is fresh. Yesterday's rain hasn't touched it.

A woman's voice comes down the stair from the half-open door above, sharp, worn thin by repeating itself: "I've told you once already. Nothing leaves that room till I'm paid."

A man answers her, too low to make out.

Where you are: at the cooper's yard gate, off the Coast Way · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 3 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You caught Pell's eye and pointed briefly at the chalk mark, leaving it untouched. Then you went through the half-open gate with your sword sheathed and your shield on your arm. The yard smells of wet oak and shavings, and a brazier stands there for heating hoops. At the back a broad, bald man in a leather apron stands at a hooping block with a mallet raised. When he saw you, the mallet stayed up. At the foot of the outside stair you called up the wall, in a voice made for carrying down a line of wagons, to Mistress Pike. You gave your name, said you and your companions had a letter from Ostrin Vell about his strongbox, and added that you ought to talk before anything got carried away.

The argument upstairs stopped dead. The cooper brought his mallet down on the hoop once more, carefully, as if he had never paused.

Just short of the gate, Sefa stepped back into the narrow shade beside the barrel stack, her hands still at her sides and her eyes on the door above. She spoke very low, to Pell. Pell crouched by the gatepost as if he had a stone in his boot, then straightened and looked the street over once. He slipped through the gate behind you and took the stair on the wall side, where the treads are nailed tightest, while every eye above was turned toward you at the bottom.

Near the top, one tread is new pale pine, nailed over the stump of an old one, and it sits a finger higher than the rest. Pell's heel catches its edge and the plank gives a dry crack. In the noise of the yard it's a small sound, but nobody up there is talking.

A woman steps out onto the landing first: thin, about fifty, sleeves pushed to the elbow, a ring of keys hanging from her belt on a leather thong. She looks down over the rail at you. A man moves into the half-open doorway behind her, unhurried, and his eyes go straight down the stair to Pell, three treads below his boots.

He is past forty, lean, with grey hair cropped close and a nose that was broken once and set a little crooked. He wears a good plain coat and has a short cudgel hooked in his belt. He holds a small purse in his left hand, half open, the way a man holds something he has been showing. He looks at Pell a breath longer than he needs to, then smiles.

"Mind that one, friend. It's new." His voice is soft and pleasant, with the vowels of the Lower City docks. "The old one went through under the men carrying him down." He looks down at you, then past you to the barrel stack where Sefa stands in the shade, and he counts the three of you without hiding it. He speaks to the landlady without raising his voice. "Three of them now, mistress. My offer hasn't changed, and it's in my hand. Theirs is a letter."

The landlady doesn't look round at him. She grips the rail and speaks down to you in a thin, worn voice. "Halloway. I don't know you. I know Jassan Ferr owed me three gold and four silver. I know his master paid the temple to bury him and never sent me a copper for the room he died in. I've sold the man's good coat to cover part of it, and I'm not ashamed of that." Her other hand closes over the keys at her belt. "Nothing leaves that room till I'm paid. I said it to him and I'll say it to you, Vell's letter or no."

Below, the cooper's mallet strikes the hoop, and strikes it again.

(While the others were looking elsewhere, a boy pressed a sealed letter into your hand and was gone before anyone else saw. It is for you alone. You break the seal and read:)

«Bram — Harl died owing Ostrin Vell forty gold, and Vell's note for it is in his dead clerk's strongbox — the one Vell has hired you to bring him. Jassan wrote to me before he died: once the box is back, Vell calls the note and takes the house. If that one page were gone before Vell opened the box, there would be nothing to call. Please. I have no one else to ask. — Odda Brand»

Where you are: at the foot of the outside stair in the cooper's yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 4 — what does Bram Halloway do?

As you finish speaking, Pell has already come up past the new pine tread to the landing, and nods to the grey-haired man as he passes. Then she went on up. Pell gave Coll a short nod from the bottom step and said a roof-cant line about a long wait on a short step. At the top he dropped two coppers in the old man's basket and asked the sister about Brother Aldane, mentioning the clerk Jassan Ferr and something of his that the brother ought to see.

Coll stepped back off the bottom step onto the dust of the road, and his two men eased back onto the verges. "Off the stone, mistress. I've no quarrel with the Morninglord." To Pell's line he answered quietly in the same cant that the sun was long today, which means he can wait as long as you can. After that he watched the road, not the doors.

The old man with the crutch looked up, surprised, at the coppers. "Dawn keep you, lad." The young freckled sister, her rose hem grey with step-dust, looked from your mail to the iron-cornered box to the green wax. Brother Aldane was in the infirmary, she said, and she led you in, warning you to ignore the novices, who stare at anyone in armour.

The nave was cool and smelled of beeswax and lime. Amber and rose light from the east window lay across kneeling townsfolk, none of whom looked at the box. Down a side passage two novices folding bandages stopped to watch you go by. The sister brought you to a long whitewashed room with six cots, four empty, and shelves of stoppered jars. An old woman slept in the end cot. The window looks south onto the herb beds, and neither road nor steps can be seen from it. The sister announced you and went back to her broom.

You set the box down by the worktable with the green wax facing up and away from everyone's hands, swung the shield onto your arm, and stood with a boot against the oak. Pell told you and Sefa in a low voice: the box stays with you, nobody touches the wax, you show it and don't hand it over, and he keeps the stamp on him until he says otherwise.

Brother Aldane finished a turn of his pestle before putting it down. He is past sixty, broad, with big clean hands, short white hair, a rose stole, and a linen apron stained green-brown. He looked the three of you over, the box last. Sefa greeted him, and Pell held out the cloth-wrapped vial, cork in, and asked what it was, what too much would do, what Aldane saw on the body, and who sells such a thing.

Aldane didn't take it. It was his own foxglove steeped in spirit, made for Jassan at the thaw for a stumbling heart: three drops in water at night. Too much brings sickness, yellow rings round candles, and a heart that goes wrong in a way you feel. Jassan had no sick on him, and a finger gone from the bottle is about a month's use, so he took no excess and nobody dosed him. His lips and nails were grey-blue and his hands cold to the wrist, as with any stopped heart. His eyes had been closed by Wenna before Aldane came. He smelled only of drops and old paper, with no marks on throat or wrists; Aldane looked because Vell paid for the burial. Nobody sells the drops. He makes them for the infirmary, and herb-wives won't touch foxglove.

To Sefa, more gently, he said he spoke the dawn words over Jassan in his chair and the room was just a room; a death doesn't foul a place. Then he knelt with a grunt beside the box and studied the seal from a forearm's length without touching it.

"That's not funeral wax. Those are Waukeen's scales, the old way of drawing them. My father kept a bond from her house in the Gate, green wax like this, from before she went quiet in the Troubles." The closed eye under the beam troubled him: "The eye wasn't on his. I've never seen that."

He rose slowly, wiping clean hands again. Jassan came the day before he died, not for his drops, sat in the second pew from the noon bell until the light left the east window, then came back and asked Aldane something he has thought about every day since. He will tell you what, but first he wants to know why three armed people bring a dead clerk's box to a temple instead of to Ostrin Vell, with a man and two bruisers waiting at the foot of his steps. He and the sister saw them from the porch.

The old woman sighed and turned to the wall. A bee worked along the sage outside, and the green wax caught the light from the herb beds.

Where you are: temple infirmary, by the worktable with Brother Aldane · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 13 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa speaks first, the way a novice reports to a senior sister. She tells Brother Aldane you were hired to carry a box, and that on the road it stopped being the one the employer described. Vell promised red-brown wax, but the wax is green, and it corresponds to a lead stamp the clerk kept hidden beneath his floorboards. She says you haven't broken it or sold it, though Coll Brannock, who waited on the road and named no master, has put eighty gold on offer for taking it away intact, and a hundred and twenty if you say where it was found and whose seal it bears. She says she wanted the man who laid hands on Jassan to look at it and say whether the death and the seal belonged together. She adds that Vell will pay for delivery, but that if this is Waukeen's scales, it is a merchant's keeping, and she'd like to know whose bargain it is.

Pell takes the vial back and slips it into his satchel away from the red flasks, then answers the priest straight, keeping his voice low for the novices in the passage. He tells of Vell's commission, the red-brown wax with a ring V that Vell described twice, and the green seal found instead. He says he wanted to know whether Jassan died on his own and what you are carrying, and thanks the priest for the answer to the first. He says the man at the foot of the steps works for a moneylender on the Trade Way and has followed you since the cooper's yard, and that you are not selling. He mentions no stamp of his own. He asks what Jassan asked, then whether anyone in the Lower City still seals in green the old way, and who a letter sent "care of" someone might be.

You then say your own piece, quietly over the sleeping woman, and ask what Jassan asked.

Aldane has heard all of you out without interrupting. When Sefa mentioned the stamp under the floorboards, he glanced at the box, then at the three of you, and didn't ask to see it. His eyes rest on Pell a moment longer than on the others, and then he lets it go.

"A widow," he says to you. "Which?" At the name he nods slowly. "Odda Brand. I know her hands. She brings the boy in with his chest every winter. A debt is between the people who signed for it. I won't tell you what to do with a box I've not been asked to carry."

He pulls a stool from under the worktable and sits heavily, forearms on his apron. He looks older sitting down.

"He asked me this: is a man guilty for what he writes down for others?" He says it like a dose read off a jar. "A clerk writes the sum he's given. He doesn't lend, doesn't sign the note, doesn't call it in. He only writes it true. So is he part of what comes after?" He looks at his hands. "I told him a clerk who writes a true sum and doesn't know what it's for has done his work, and no more. But one who comes to know what it's for and keeps writing has a different question, and should take it to whoever the sums are hurting, not to a priest." The old woman in the end cot murmurs, and he waits until she is still. "He thought a long while. Then he said, 'And if I've written it twice?' I asked what he meant by twice. He thanked me for the drops and went."

He rises, takes a twist of cloth from a small drawer under the shelf of jars, and unrolls it by the mortar. Three silver coins lie in it, thicker than Beregost silver and worn smooth at the rims, each stamped with a squat tower over a crossed line and lettering nearly worn away.

"He put these in the alms box on his way out. Sister Ivet brought them to me because she didn't know them." He pushes one toward the light. "Zhentil Keep. The old mint, from before the Keep was pulled down. You see them on the Moonsea. Here, never. I kept them out of the poor-box because a beggar who tried to spend one would be asked where he got it."

You have seen that tower before, on the Amn run, in the purses of northern outriders who guarded wagons nobody asked questions about. Caravan men called the coin black silver and didn't like taking it, because of who it came from.

Aldane answers Pell's last questions plainly. He doesn't know who seals in green the old way in the Gate; he hasn't been north of the Wyrm's Rock in thirty years. Waukeen's house there shut when she went silent in the Troubles, and when she returned her new priests wanted nothing to do with the old clerks or their bonds. His father's bond was never honoured; he kept it in a drawer till he died. He rolls the cloth back over the coins and leaves them on the table. "'Care of' somebody in the Lower City. That's a man who doesn't want his own name on the outside of a letter. Beyond that I can't help you."

He looks down at the green seal on the floor by your boot a while longer. "He died in his chair of his own heart. I'll stand by that." He says it to all three of you. "But he sat in my second pew for four hours first. Nobody does that over a sum he's sure of."

Down the passage the two novices have given up folding bandages and are whispering. On the porch the sister's broom starts again, slow over the stone. The bee has left the sage for the rosemary. The old woman sleeps with her face to the wall. The coins lie in their cloth beside the mortar, and on the floor the closed eye under the scales faces the whitewashed ceiling.

Where you are: temple infirmary with Brother Aldane · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 14 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Pell looked at the three coins for a long while without touching them, then at the box. Half to himself, he said Jassan had kept two books: one for Vell, and a faithful copy of what the sums were really for. To Aldane he said that Zhentarim-style silver turning up in the poor-box, caravans that never reach Nashkel, and a clerk sitting four hours in a pew did not sit well with him. He thanked the priest and asked two last things: did Jassan name anyone or say where he was going, and would Aldane keep the coins just as they are. Then he spoke low to you and Sefa. The box stays here, you walk out with empty hands, and you go to Feldepost's coach yard and then to Dobbin at the Juggler. He asked Aldane whether the Song would hold the sealed box in its infirmary until the afternoon.

Sefa stood still while the cloth was rolled over the silver. She said a man who thought himself guilty would shed such coins like a fever, and that she had seen men do the same with wages from a trade they'd come to call a sin. She paced once between the table and the window and gave her reading of the seal: a bargain in two parts, one hand of two, with the other meant to see who opened it. Jassan, she said, wanted it opened by the proper person at the proper moment. She told Aldane he had given Jassan a good answer, better than Jassan could carry. She asked him to keep the coins apart and his word about the body close, and asked whether there was a way off the hill that avoided the front steps.

Aldane heard you all out on his stool and answered in order. Jassan named no one and did not say where he was going. At the door he had asked one thing: whether the Fist ever comes to the dawn rite. Aldane told him one sergeant, Cowl, does, most mornings, sits at the back and leaves before the hymn. He put the twist of cloth in the small drawer under the jars and shut it. The coins stay as they are, he said, and nobody spends them.

To Pell he said no to keeping the box alone. He would not be its keeper. It can sit by the empty cot beside the worktable as long as one of you sits with it, and no one will lay a hand on it while he is in the room.

To you he said he wouldn't come to Vell's counter, since he has the old woman to tend, and tipped his head at the end cot. But he would write down what he saw. His broad, slow hand, a hand that labels jars, put down that an oak strongbox, iron at the corners, sealed over the lock in dark green wax upon lead, the mark a pair of scales above a closed eye, whole and unbroken, was brought by Bram Halloway and two others who carry it for Ostrin Vell. He signed it as Aldane of the Morninglord's house, sealed it with rose-coloured wax and a small brass sun, and laid it by the mortar. What Vell asks for Mistress Brand's roof is between you and Vell, he said, but he would like to know the answer.

To Sefa he was just as plain. He will keep the coins apart, but not his word about the body. If the Fist or Vell asks, he will say the man's own heart stopped. The way off the hill is the little gate at the bottom of the sage, into the burial ground where Jassan's new mound lies by the yew. Past the graves a lane runs round the hill and comes out on the Trade Way by the first houses to the north. It isn't hidden.

You all look. Past the sage and rosemary a hurdle gate stands in a low wall, and beyond it the burial ground slopes away under a single dark yew, with a fresh brown mound at its foot. At the far side, where the lane runs off, a man thick through the shoulders sits on the boundary wall in a carter's smock that doesn't fit him, boots dangling over the lane, working through one of the almshouse rolls.

In the end cot the old woman wakes, blinks at the whitewash and turns her head until she finds you, the man in mail. She tells you that if you've come to carry her out, you can wait, for she hasn't had her bread. Aldane is already filling a cup at the ewer. On the worktable lie the priest's note under its rose-coloured wax and the shut drawer with the black silver. By your boot the green eye on the box faces the ceiling.

Where you are: infirmary of the Song of the Morning, by the box · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 15 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You take the folded note from beside the mortar. The rose wax is still a little soft under your thumb. You tuck it away, draw a stool out from under the end of the worktable and set it by the box. The old woman looks over your mail, your shield and the oak box at your boots, and seems to decide you'll do as furniture. She tells you to wait quieter, since you creak. Pell reaches for the same note a moment after you and finds bare wood. He turns the movement into a small bow toward the end cot and says he is not carrying her anywhere, only boxes. She doesn't answer. Aldane has given her a cup of water and a roll from the almshouse basket, and she has better things to do.

You give your piece in a low voice: you'll stay with the box, the other two can follow up the coach yard and Dobbin, and they should ask where Sergeant Cowl is found. You warn them that the smock man is on the burial-ground lane, so that way isn't clear, and that they should be back well before dusk. You set the shield against your knee and put one boot against the oak.

Sefa has moved to the window and stands to one side of it, so the light falls on her shoulder and not her face. Past the sage and the hurdle gate the man in the smock is still on the boundary wall, boots hanging over the lane, picking crumbs off his front. She says what she sees and what she'd do. The box stays with you. She and Pell leave the way they came, empty-handed, and go to Feldepost's for the name on Jassan's letters. If anyone follows them, they'll split in the alley by the Juggler. Then she turns to Aldane with a question about Jassan and Cowl, and a half-smile to soften it.

Aldane has gone back to his stool. He thinks before he answers. He can't say what was in Jassan, he says, only how he asked. Jassan had his hat on and his hand on the door, and he wanted to know if the Fist attended the dawn rite. Aldane told him about Cowl. Then Jassan asked at which bell the rite begins, and Aldane said the first. Jassan said "Tomorrow, then," not to him, the way a man tells himself where he's put his boots. He was dead before the first bell, and Wenna Pike's man came for Aldane at second.

Pell has already gone. While Sefa was still putting her question, he said the rest of his plan low at your shoulder: you stay with the box, Sefa comes or stays as she likes, and the stamp stays on him. If he isn't back by the afternoon bell, you carry the box to Vell with the priest's note and don't come looking. Then he went down the side passage, past the two novices, who went back to their bandages in a hurry, and out through the nave.

The bee has gone from the rosemary. The old woman eats her roll in small, careful bites. You sit with the box against your boot and the shield at your knee, and Sefa stands at the window. On the boundary wall beyond the yew, the man in the smock hasn't moved.

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Brother Aldane's witness note

Where you are: infirmary, beside the box · Time: Day 1 · morning

The session is over.
